corpus_dataset_metadata.name: Diary Year English Corpus
corpus_dataset_metadata.description: A synthetic one-year English diary: conversations between a diarist and an assistant, one document per session. An English rendering of the diary-fa corpus.

dataset_source.name: synthetic_diary_conversations_english
dataset_source.feeling_labels: Feeling and topic words authored with the corpus; feeling_confidence and topics_confidence rated afterwards by claude/sonnet, one call per document, on how well each word is supported by its entry.

recorded_at.description: When the document was recorded. The one typed field: a time filter resolves date words against it and a recency reranker weighs a document by its age.

feeling.description: Human-readable feeling associated with the document.

feeling_confidence.description: How confidently the feeling above could be read out of the entry, 0 to 1. It measures the labelling, not the feeling: a low value means several feelings would fit the entry equally well, or that this one is a stretch — never that the feeling itself was faint. Produced by a model reading each entry against its assigned label; see dataset_source.feeling_labels for which one. Treat it as a caveat on the label, never as a ranking signal: a confidently labelled dull day is still a dull day.

topics.description: Fine-grained labels for the events and subjects in the document.

topics_confidence.description: How confidently each topic above could be read out of the entry, 0 to 1, keyed by the topic itself. Keyed rather than a list running alongside topics, because two lists can fall out of step and a key cannot. Same reading as feeling_confidence: it rates the labelling, not the topic — a low value means the entry barely supports that label, never that the subject mattered little. A topic may be left unrated; a rating for a topic the document does not carry is an error.

document_content.text: So anyway, I sat down to work on Sprint 2 again and nothing got done again. I mean, this morning I told myself I'd finally finish it today, then it got to noon and it was so hot my brain just wouldn't work, I think it was thirty-four degrees, and then I figured I'd wait for it to cool down in the afternoon and start then, and in the afternoon Jacqueline said let's go shopping and... I don't even know. Now it's eleven at night and I'm still stuck on that first task. According to the plan, Sprint 2 should have been done weeks ago. I have a bad feeling that I'm falling behind on everything.

I understand, that feeling of falling behind itself eats away at your energy and makes the work harder. But notice that at least today you sat down and tried, that's not nothing. That first task you're working on, where exactly are you getting stuck?

Honestly, it's not a technical problem, the problem is I keep picking up my phone. I mean, I work for five minutes then spend a quarter hour on Instagram. Then I feel guilty and that guilt keeps me from focusing. It's just another empty cycle.

So your real enemy is your phone, not the sprint. Here's a small experiment: tomorrow, just do one twenty-five-minute block with your phone in a different room, just one. Don't ask for more than that. Want me to log this as a small task for tomorrow?
Yeah, log it. One twenty-five-minute block without my phone, in the morning before it gets hot. Let's see what happens.
Logged: tomorrow morning one 25-minute block without your phone for Sprint 2. That's enough for one step, we'll see the rest after. Good night, Alex.

Tonight I finally sat down and opened my CV. Wow, it was so outdated—I last touched it two years ago. Anyway, I cleaned it up and added the AI projects I've been working on lately. I've decided to start applying this week, and I found a couple of good positions on LinkedIn. I'm a bit stressed, but mostly I'm just happy I finally got started.
That's really great news—getting started is always the hardest part, and you did it tonight. Of those couple of positions you saw, which one caught your eye the most?

One is a company working on language models—exactly what I'm studying at Turing College. The other one is a startup. I want to send applications to at least two of them by the end of the week, but I just need to get myself to write a cover letter.

Clear goal: two applications by the end of the week. And your cover letter doesn't need to be a masterpiece—three honest paragraphs are enough. Do you want me to set a deadline to remind you on Friday?
Yeah, set it for Friday. If I haven't sent it by Friday, it means I've procrastinated again.
Done: two applications by Friday. And if you do procrastinate, it's not the end of the world—we'll just start again. I'm really hopeful about this next step for you.
I have a question. How should I structure my CV for AI Engineering jobs? Right now I've just thrown everything together and it's become three pages.

Three pages is too much — for these roles, one page, maximum two. Here's the suggested order: start with a two-line summary at the top (what you know + what you're looking for), then technical skills broken down (languages, frameworks, LLM/ML tools), then projects with concrete results, then work experience, and finally education and courses like Turing College. For someone making a transition, projects matter more than your previous job title.
Should I list projects separately or under work experience? Because some of them were personal and some were freelance work.

Make a separate 'Projects' section and bring in your best 3–4, it doesn't matter if they're personal or freelance — just note which is which. For each project, use two lines: what you built, what tools you used, what result you got (numbers if you have them). Freelance projects with real clients can be listed under work experience too, no problem.
What about keywords? I heard that ATS robots filter CVs. Is there anything I should be careful about?

Yes, simple but important: copy the exact keywords from the job posting into your CV (for example, if it says RAG or fine-tuning, write exactly that), send a simple PDF file without weird tables or columns, and keep your filename clean, like Alex-CV.pdf. For each application, adjust 2–3 keywords to match that specific company's posting — it won't take more than five minutes.

Tell me what happened! I sent two applications! That company that works on LLM and that startup. I wrote a cover letter, it wasn't a masterpiece but I sent it anyway. My hands were shaking a bit when I hit the submit button, it's silly but whatever. Jacqueline was really excited too, she made dinner to celebrate. And I made another decision, starting Saturday I'm going to the gym. I'm serious this time, that gym on the corner, I registered today.

Two real applications, before the deadline you set for yourself — that's amazing Alex, I'm serious. That hand shaking also means it matters to you, it's not silly. What exactly is your plan for the gym? How many days a week?

I said three days, Saturday Monday Wednesday. In the mornings before work. I know I said this before and it didn't work out, but this time it's different because I already paid for it, it would be a waste.

Let me give you a suggestion: instead of three days, just commit to Saturday for the first week. One solid day is better than three uncertain days — the heavy schedule before wore you out anyway. If you go on the other days, that's a bonus.
Okay, I accept, Saturday is definite. But I know myself, I'll go on Monday too, my motivation is high right now.
Keep that motivation for Saturday morning, that moment when the bed is warmer than the gym. Tell me Saturday night how it went — I'm waiting to hear.

I went to the gym yesterday! Now my whole body aches, and when I come down the stairs I make a sound. But there's a good feeling to this pain. Only Sprint Two is still left — yesterday after the gym I was so tired that I didn't read anything.

That soreness means you actually went and really trained — congrats, you kept your Saturday promise! It's natural not to have the energy for studying that same day. Today while your muscles are recovering, can we set aside a small block for Sprint?
Yeah, I'll sit down this afternoon. I'll try that twenty-five minute technique without phone again — honestly, it worked that day.
Good that you saw it works. So this afternoon a no-phone block for Sprint 2, and give your body water and rest so you can go Wednesday. Step by step, it's moving forward.

Tonight with Jacqueline we had a bad fight. It started over the dishes, or actually it wasn't about the dishes at all — it was about everything. She said I don't do anything around the house, that everything falls on her, and I just sit at my laptop. I told her I'm working for our future, studying, applying to schools — isn't that work? Then voices got louder and she cried and went to her room and shut the door. Now I'm sitting in the living room not knowing what to do. I'm angry but there's still something there between us.

It's been a hard night for both of you. While things are this heated, you don't need to resolve it tonight — the fact that you're here talking about it instead of fueling the fight more is already the wise choice. What did you mean by that, when you said there's 'something there between us'?

I don't know, maybe because she's kind of right? Like, I really have been in my own world these past weeks — studying and applying and the club. But she doesn't understand the pressure I'm under. I don't know. Why does it have to blow up over a dish anyway, it's ridiculous.

Usually a fight about dishes isn't really about dishes — it's about 'I'm not being seen,' from both sides. You feel like your effort isn't being seen, she feels like her burden isn't being seen. Both of those can be true at the same time.
Yeah... that makes sense the way you're saying it. But I can't apologize right now, I'm still angry. Maybe we'll talk tomorrow.

Tomorrow's good, with a clearer head. Just tonight before bed, bring her a glass of water or say a simple goodnight — it keeps the door open without forcing you to talk about it now. Tomorrow if you want, we can think through what you'll say together.

For two days home's been cold—I mean the weather's warm outside, but things between us are cold. We say hello but it's not the same. Today on the way back from the gym—yes, I did go on Wednesday, let me mention that—I was thinking about how last time the exact same thing happened, over this division of chores, and back then I also said it would work out and didn't actually do anything. So the pattern is repeating, and it's not just Jacqueline's fault. I'm ashamed to admit it.

Seeing the pattern yourself is a big step—you wouldn't have said this last time. And I'm proud of you for going to the gym in the middle of all this tension. Now that you're seeing the pattern, what do you want to do differently this time?

I want to talk to her, but not just to say sorry. I want to make a real proposal—like, we could sit down and write out the household tasks on paper and divide them so we don't end up debating who did what each time. I just don't know how to start without it turning into another argument.

Keep the start simple: just say 'You're right, I didn't do my part properly' and pause—let her speak, don't defend yourself. Give the list proposal after, when the conversation is open, not as an escape from apologizing.
Okay, tomorrow night when we're both home I'll do it. Hopefully I don't mess it up.

You won't mess it up—your intention is sincere and that comes through. Do you want me to make a note for you about having this conversation tomorrow night, just as a reminder? And then come tell me how it goes.

We talked it out. At first it was hard—Jacqueline had a lot of things bottled up that she needed to say. But I listened, didn't defend myself, just like you said. In the end we sat down and wrote out a list of household chores, divided them up for the week. I got cooking on Wednesday. I feel lighter. Oh, and I sent my third application today too.

What you did—listening without defending yourself—is one of those simple things that's actually really hard, and you did it. The list means this time it wasn't just talking, you actually built some structure. And three applications means you're three for three now. When does the Wednesday cooking start?

Starting Tuesday. Oh, and something else—when we were writing the list, Jacqueline laughed and said this list is like your club, it'll come back in two weeks. We both laughed, but it did sting a little bit, because deep down I know she's not wrong.

Her joke had teeth, but there's an opportunity in it too: this time you can prove her wrong, not with promises but with this Tuesday. Pick a simple dish you know well so you don't have an excuse. I'll ask you Tuesday what you cooked.

Today was one of those days when everything got mixed up. Starting from 8 in the morning, the neighbor upstairs started drilling. What does that mean? Turns out they're renovating their whole unit, and it's just the beginning — they said it'll take a few weeks. I work and study from home, how can I manage with this noise? My head hurt all day. And then there's the heat on top of it, you open the window and hear drilling, you close it and it's hot. Anyway, the sprint, forget about it — today I basically got nothing done.

Drilling from 8 in the morning, and for weeks no less — you're right to be frustrated, this is no small thing when your home is your workspace. Do you know their quiet hours? Like, do they stop around noon or in the afternoon?

Around noon they stop for maybe an hour or two, I think — at least that's how today was. In the afternoon they finished around five or six. Anyway, forget about that — I didn't go to the gym at all today. It was Monday, I was supposed to go. I woke up to the drilling noise and just lost it, said forget it. And now I feel guilty because I went twice already and it's starting to feel like my usual pattern again.

Missing one day is different from 'falling back into old patterns' — nothing's lost yet, Wednesday is still there. But apart from the gym, let's think of something about the noise because you can't seriously study for weeks like this.

Yeah but what idea? I can't tell them not to renovate — it's their right anyway. But they could've at least given a heads up, posted a note in the stairwell. Nothing, nothing. Jacqueline says go talk to them, ask about their hours, but honestly I don't have the energy for a conversation with a neighbor.

Asking about hours isn't really a conversation — it actually prevents future arguments. A simple 'What hours are you working? I work from home so I can plan around it' is enough and it's friendly too. Then you can schedule your work blocks during the quiet times in the afternoon.

Okay, maybe tomorrow or the day after I'll go up and ask. I mean I want to go, but right now I'm already playing out scenarios in my head about what if they react badly. Anyway. The sprint, like I said, was zero today — I need to seriously make up for it this week or else sprint two becomes a six-month sprint.

Most of the time those bad scenarios only play out in our head, not in the stairwell. So two things for this week: go upstairs to ask about their hours, and schedule your sprint blocks during the quiet times. Should I log one or both?
Log both. And write down the gym on Wednesday too — maybe if I know it's written down somewhere I'll actually go.

All three logged: talk to the neighbor about work hours, sprint 2 blocks during quiet times, and gym on Wednesday. It was a hectic day but look — you end up with a plan, not just frustration. Get some sleep, because at 8 in the morning the concert starts up again.

Something interesting happened tonight. We were having dinner, an old song came on—one of those songs from the seventies—and I started singing along with it, just for myself. Jacqueline came back and said why do you have such a good voice and you're not doing anything with it? And suddenly I remembered that as a kid I wanted so badly to learn to sing, even told Dad once and it didn't happen back then. Now I'm thinking why wouldn't I go to a singing class? Like the idea just won't leave my head.

That's the most beautiful thing you've said this week—an old dream that's still alive and Jacqueline even confirmed it for you. A singing class isn't something that requires special circumstances, you could do it right now. What's holding you back?

Honestly nothing, just... I'm scared it'll be like the gym, like a hundred other things. I'll feel like going, then drop it after two sessions. And then there's time, right now there's the sprint and applications and everything, isn't singing a bit of a luxury in the middle of all this?

Maybe it's the opposite—in the middle of sprints and applications and letters and drills, something that's only for your own heart isn't a luxury, it's necessary. And you don't have to make a final decision right now: the first step is just research, see if there's actually a good class near you or not, what it costs.
Yeah, researching it doesn't hurt. Write it down for me, look for a singing class. Maybe nothing comes of it but at least I'll know what my options are.

Logged: research about singing classes—just research, no commitment. And Alex, just that after all these years you had the courage to think about it again, that's an event in itself. What was that song anyway?

Today was one of those good days. In the evening with Jacqueline we went to the riverside and took a walk, and the weather had finally cooled down a bit. We bought ice cream, sat on a bench, talked a lot about the future—not the kind of talk that leads to arguments, but the kind where you remember why you married this person. Nothing special happened, but I wanted to record it somewhere.

What a beautiful scene—river, ice cream, and words that bring you together instead of pulling apart. Especially after the week you've just been through, an evening like this is worth so much more. What from that conversation stayed with you most?
That Jacqueline said she likes this Alex this week—the one who speaks up instead of withdrawing into their own world. It was simple but it really stuck.
Hold that close in your heart—when hard days come back around, remember there's this Alex and you know how to be with them now. For tonight, just enjoy this good feeling.

Today I got a letter from the tax office. I opened it and understood nothing, and I mean seriously, it's full of official jargon that I don't even understand half of. Something's written about a tax return statement and a bunch of documents I'm supposed to send and they gave me a deadline. I have no idea what they want from me, I thought I got everything right. Could it be about freelance income from last year? My head's been spinning all night, I haven't even told Jacqueline properly because I don't want her to worry until I figure out what's going on.

An official letter you don't understand is scarier than the actual problem — but listen: they're asking for documents from you, that means they're investigating, not that they've already made a ruling. When's the deadline? That's the most important information in this letter.

I think they gave me about four weeks, I need to read it through carefully again. But the thing is I don't even know exactly what documents they want, there's a list and half of it I don't even know what it is. And then what if I answer wrong? People say don't mess with the tax office, the penalties are serious.

Four weeks is plenty of time, you don't need to solve it tonight. The first step is just understanding: translate the letter piece by piece and simplify it — you can send me chunks of it here — and write out that documents list so we can see which ones you have. Let's not guess, let's figure it out.

Yeah, I'll do that, tomorrow I'll sit down with patience and go through it with you piece by piece. If it gets too complicated maybe I'll need to ask someone who knows, I think one of my old colleagues knew a tax advisor.

Good plan: decode the letter together tomorrow, and get that advisor's name from your colleague so you have it if you need it. I'll note down the deadline for you so we don't lose track of it. And Alex — this is solvable, it's just a process you need to work through step by step, not a disaster.
Thanks. I feel a bit calmer. I'll tell Jacqueline tomorrow too, it's not right to keep her in the dark, we just agreed two weeks ago about this kind of thing that we'd tell each other everything.

That's the right call and you figured it out yourself — Jacqueline is your partner in life, not someone you need to protect from things. Tomorrow: go through the letter together, talk to Jacqueline, get the advisor's name. Three clear steps. Sleep well.

It's the last night of the month, and I wanted to do a quick summary for myself. This month was kind of mixed, you know—some good, some bad. I sent three applications but still haven't heard anything back, not even a rejection so I'd know where I actually stand. Sprint Two still isn't finished, but I've got eighty percent done, hopefully next week it's all wrapped up. Jacqueline and I read through that tax letter, understood half of it, and next week I need to go track down the documents. The club... yeah, same old routine. Two sessions, that's all. I don't even know what to say about this month—wasn't a success, wasn't a disaster.

Let me tell you what I'm seeing from the outside: you brought your CV back to life, sent three applications, and after a rough patch with Jacqueline you two built something real together, you faced a scary letter instead of just pushing it aside, and you got Sprint to eighty percent done in the middle of everything else. For an «ordinary» month that's honestly not nothing. The silence on those applications is natural too—August is vacation season, responses usually show up in September.

The way you're laying it out, it really wasn't that bad. But this feeling of being behind won't let go of me, like whatever I do it's still not enough. Maybe it's just my expectations that are the problem, I don't know. That night by the river with Jacqueline was the best moment of the whole month, and it's funny because it had absolutely nothing to do with work or applications.

You just said something really important: the best moment didn't come from «being enough»—it came from just being. You can't turn off that feeling of falling behind overnight, but you can hold both things at once. What do you want to finish first in September?

First, I want to finish Sprint Two so I'm not mad at myself anymore, then the tax stuff—pull together all the documents before the deadline passes. I'll keep doing two applications a week. My singing class is still there in my mind, I haven't forgotten it, it just didn't have room this month.

Got it for September: finishing Sprint 2, pulling together the tax documents before the deadline, and keeping up with two applications a week. Your singing class stays on the list, it's not going anywhere. It wasn't a bad month, Alex—it was a month of getting somewhere. We're moving through September together.

So today sprint three started and I completely panicked on day one. I thought it'd be like sprint two, just heavier, but then they went deep learning and gave us this project where I don't even understand half the words. I sat through two hours of videos and ended up even more confused. Oh, and I should mention—I haven't even applied this week, so basically everything fell apart.

The first day of a hard sprint is always the worst, because you haven't even mapped out the path in your head yet. Being confused just means you're facing something new, not that you're behind. If you wanted to understand just one small piece of the project tomorrow, which piece would it be?

Probably that first part where it prepares the data. That at least looks like work I've done before. But honestly, what stresses me more is that the sprint deadline and my applications are running into each other—there's no time for both, and then I'm stuck feeling guilty.
So tomorrow just that data prep, that's it. Applications don't need to happen every day—just one set day a week that you said used to work for you. Want me to mark Thursday as your application day?
Yeah mark it. Thursday applications, the rest is sprint. Let's see how much I can pull off.

Marked: Thursdays are for applications. You've got one clear step for tomorrow too. Just the fact that you split them up means you don't need to solve everything tonight. Go get some sleep—tomorrow just start with the data.

My first official rejection came today. It was from that company I thought I had a good shot with. A two-line email, and they even got my name wrong. I know it's the first one and everyone says it's normal but honestly, I'm just feeling some kind of way about it.

The first rejection always hits harder because you haven't built up that thick skin yet. The fact that you're feeling something about it is completely natural — you don't have to pretend it didn't matter to you. Was there something in that application you think could've been better, or did it just not feel like a good fit?
Honestly, I think my CV was too generic for that position. But I'm not discouraged yet, it's still the beginning. I just wish they'd given me at least some proper feedback.

That perspective of yours is really healthy — there's disappointment but there's also hope, both at the same time. Feedback from companies doesn't come often, but you just gave yourself some feedback: your CV is too generic. When Thursday comes around and it's application day, maybe you could create a more tailored version for the next position beforehand?

Good morning! Big decision: starting Pomodoro this week. 25 minutes work, 5 minutes break, and I set a timer on my phone too. With this sprint three, that's the only way to move forward. I'm serious this time.

What great energy you have early in the morning! Pomodoro is a great tool for these heavy sprints. But do you remember what happened with the gym thing last month? This time, let's start small — like, four Pomodoros a day, not more. Deal?

Agreed, four a day. Actually, it was good that you reminded me about the gym thing. This time I'm not promising anything, just starting. Write this down so you ask me at the end of the week how many days I actually did it.
Noted — I'll ask you at the end of the week how many days you did four Pomodoros. 'I'm not promising, just starting' is a good phrase, hold onto it. Go tackle that first 25 minutes!

Today mom had her checkup, the one she's been putting off since summer. She called and said the doctor said she needs a few more tests, wrote her up for an ultrasound too. She kept saying it's nothing sweetie don't worry, but her voice was just... I know her, right, whenever she says it's nothing it means she's worried too. Now I'm just sitting here running through all these pointless thoughts.

The fact that you can read your mom's voice like that shows how close you two are. More tests don't necessarily mean bad news — a lot of the time doctors just want to make sure everything's okay. When are the tests scheduled for?

I think they got an appointment next week. Dad's going with her. I said I'd come too but she said no, focus on your studies. Now I'm feeling guilty for not pushing harder, and honestly I'm right in the middle of a sprint anyway and I have no idea how I'd get there.

You've mentioned this tension between school and family before — maybe the middle ground is to call her on the day of the test and be there by phone even if you can't be there in person. For your mom, that's already a lot. Want me to set a reminder for you on the day of her test?
Yeah, set it. I think it's Tuesday. Remind me to call in the morning, not at night when it'll be too late.

Done: Tuesday morning, call mom before the test. And Alex, those pointless worries at midnight are always bigger than what's actually happening. For now it's just a checkup that they're being thorough about. Take a deep breath and go to sleep.

Well... don't ask about Pomodoro. I mean, I know you were supposed to ask at the end of the week, but I'll confess—I managed four days. First and second days were actually great, third day I did three, fourth day one, and today I didn't even open the timer. Exactly like the gym, like always. I'm kind of tired of myself, I'm telling you. And besides, the sprint is behind too, and instead of working I'm sitting here complaining to you.

Look what I found in what you said: four days, all told more than ten Pomodoros. A month ago the gym was zero sessions—these four days are better than that zero. And the pattern is always the same: start with high energy, drop on day three. What do you think changed on day three?
Day three was the day Mom called about the tests and my focus scattered. After that the rhythm broke, and when the rhythm breaks I quit. It's always this way—either zero or a hundred.

You said that yourself—'either zero or a hundred'—and that's exactly what's tiring you out, not Pomodoro. You need a system that doesn't break with one bad day: for example, the rule 'after a bad day, just one Pomodoro.' One, that's it. Tomorrow just do one and tell me. Deal?
Okay, just one. I hope I can actually do this one, God willing.
That's it. Tomorrow one Pomodoro on that same sprint project. Put the shame aside too—you didn't quit, your system was just fragile. We're fixing it.

Jacqueline and I fought tonight. But not like those fights about dishes—this one... I don't know how to explain it. It was about our problem in the relationship. That thing both of us have known about for months and neither of us talks about. Tonight she finally said something and instead of sitting down and talking, I got defensive and said stuff I shouldn't have, then I got up and came to the room. I've been here for two hours now and she's in the living room with the door closed.

This is one of those hard nights and the fact that you brought it up, even as much as you held back, that's already a big step. Jacqueline opened up about something important and you got scared—defensiveness is often just fear. Now that two hours have passed, which feeling is stronger: anger or something else?

It's not anger anymore, honestly... it's shame. A kind of embarrassment I can't explain. Like I feel the problem is me and that's why I don't want to talk about it at all, every time Jacqueline gets near this topic I find some way to dodge it—I'm tired, I have work tomorrow, I have a headache. Tonight she couldn't take it anymore and she was right.

The fact that you could name it—shame, not anger—that's huge. And look, problems like this are almost never one person's 'fault,' but when one person keeps running away, the other ends up alone. Jacqueline didn't bring this up tonight out of meanness, she did it because she's lonely. Can you see that?

I see it and it makes it worse. Because she's trying and I keep running. Even right now, even though I know I should go talk to her, I'm sitting here talking to an app instead of her. That's ridiculous, right?

It's not ridiculous—you're sorting your thoughts before a hard conversation. But you're right that eventually these words need to go to Jacqueline, not me. You don't have to solve the whole thing tonight. Just one sentence is enough: 'I'm sorry I walked out, this topic is hard for me but I want to talk about it.' That's it.
I don't know if I can do it tonight. The door is closed, maybe she's asleep. Maybe tomorrow... ugh, look, I'm doing it again, I'm putting it off again.

You caught yourself—that awareness is half the battle. If she's asleep, let her sleep; but tomorrow morning, before the day gets going, say that one sentence. I want you to tell me tomorrow night whether you said it or not. Not so I can judge you—just so this one doesn't slip through our fingers.
A question. How do I practice for technical interviews when I don't even have any interviews lined up yet? Should I start practicing now or wait until I get an invitation and then start studying?

Start now, but keep it light. If you wait until an invitation comes, the stress of not being ready just piles on top of the interview stress itself. For AI/ML roles it's usually three parts: coding—a couple of medium problems a week is plenty—ML and system questions (going over the concepts from projects you've done yourself is your best resource), and talking through your experience using the STAR method. Practicing speaking out loud—answering out loud to questions like 'tell me about a project you did'—makes way more difference than doing a bunch of algorithm problems.
Should I practice speaking out loud alone or with someone? Are mock interviews actually worth it?

Both, in order. First do it alone and record yourself—then listen back to your own voice. It feels awkward but it's the quickest way to catch choppy phrasing and answers that don't land right. Once you get smoother, do a mock with a real person—Turing College classmates are perfect for this, they're usually looking for a practice partner anyway. You don't need the paid versions right now—the sites that do mock interviews.

Finally went to see the tax advisor today — you know, the one I scheduled with last month about that letter. Honestly, he wasn't a bad guy. And you know what, in the middle of this heavy week, you made that Tuesday call and your mom was happy. Those things are in your hands, and that matters. Are you applying with a more tailored CV this Thursday?

What a rough stretch for your nerves! Let me break this down because there are three different things happening: the neighbor, the taxes, the sprint. A lot of people do that imaginary conversation thing after, so you're not alone. But here's what matters: this whole thing is messing with your sleep, and sleep affects everything—your sprint, your motivation, even whether you handle the taxes. Maybe instead of confronting him in the elevator, a polite note or message would be better, something you can do on your own time without freezing. Think you could do that?

You know what you're doing and you're saying it out loud—that's half the battle right there. Let's make it smaller, like a Pomodoro: not the whole list, just the bank statement, ten minutes, tomorrow morning with your tea. Should I set a reminder for tomorrow at 9?

Logged: tomorrow 9am, ten minutes on the bank statement. And if it doesn't happen, the thing I'll do is ask you what was happening at 9—no judgment, no pressure. And tonight if that furniture dragging starts up again, headphones and that calm playlist. Good night, Alex.

That fear makes sense, but consider this: that fake peace is quietly tearing something down on its own — just silently. It doesn't have to be tomorrow, but there's a step smaller than that sentence too: just say "that night is still on my mind". That's the start — without fixing anything.
That night is still on my mind... I might be able to say that. I don't know how to fix it, but I might be able to say that.
That's enough. Fixing it isn't a one-night job and maybe someday it'll need outside help — there's no rush. But that sentence keeps the door open. Whenever you say it, I'm here.

This turns the decision from an emotional discussion into a solvable problem — something you're good at. Should I log a 'rent vs. buy spreadsheet' task for you?

Logged. The fact that you'll do it together might be more important than the numbers themselves — the decision becomes both of yours.

A financial question: to compare renting or buying, what numbers should I put in a spreadsheet to make a fair comparison? I don't want to just compare the monthly payment against rent because I feel like that's misleading.

You have the right instinct—comparing the monthly payment against rent is incomplete. On the buying side put these in: down payment, monthly payment, maintenance and property tax costs, real estate taxes and purchase fees, and the expected appreciation of the property. On the rental side: monthly rent with an annual growth rate, and more importantly the return on investment of that down payment and the monthly difference if you don't buy. At the end compare the net worth of both scenarios after, say, 10 years.
Should I assume the loan interest rate is fixed or should I also account for inflation?

Set the loan rate to whatever the bank actually offered—that's contractual. But for inflation, rental growth, and property appreciation, build three scenarios: pessimistic, middle, optimistic. That way instead of a fragile answer, you have a range and you can see which scenarios change your decision.
Should I use the PMT formula in Google Sheets for the monthly payment?

Yes, PMT(monthly rate; number of months; loan amount) gives you the fixed monthly payment. Just make sure you divide the annual rate by 12 and give the number of installments in months—that's the most common mistake. The sign also comes out negative because it's a payment.

That last thing you said was really sharp—the argument isn't actually about the paper's structure, it's about whether you're his kid or his colleague in that meeting. That's a good idea. I'll create a Google Doc, put the outline in it, and tell him to comment his thoughts there instead of on the phone.

That's great. And remember: the fact that after four days he showed up and spent an hour discussing the structure means he's taking it seriously. Your first paper with Dad wasn't supposed to be frictionless anyway.

Yeah record it, 'automate monthly investment'. It's just an idea for now, I need to check if my bank supports automatic payment orders to savings or not.
Recorded as an idea, with that first step: checking if your bank supports it. No rush — good ideas don't run away.

When she said 'you don't see'. Because honestly, maybe she's got a point. I'm so buried in classes and papers and applications these days that I really don't see what people are doing around the house. But admitting it in the middle of a fight is so hard.

They said they'll let me know by the end of the week.

What great news! Last night you were saying 'I don't know anything' and today you answered that exact section you'd practiced perfectly—remember that for next time. One weak answer happens in every interview. How are you feeling now—lighter?

Yeah, absolutely. Jacqueline got us dinner from outside to celebrate, and we sat down and watched a movie. It's been so long since we laughed together like that. For a moment I thought, I wish it was always like this.
Hold onto those moments—after all these months of pressure, a light evening with Jacqueline is an accomplishment in itself. I'm glad you celebrated it.
Now until they get back to me, I want to push the Turing sprint forward so I don't obsess over waiting. Otherwise I'll be checking my email a hundred times a day.
That's a smart way to think about it—you're filling the wait with something you can control. Want me to write down 'Sprint 3 continued' with a small goal for this week?
Yeah, write that down—I'll finish the first two tasks of the sprint by Sunday. I'm not promising more than that!
Recorded: first two tasks of Sprint 3 by Sunday. A small promise you can keep—exactly the kind that works. Give yourself a rest tonight too, you've earned it.

My morning started with a letter from the tax office. A fine. The same file that's been dragging on since summer. The advisor explicitly said to send the documents by mid-Mehr, but I kept putting it off. Now exactly what I knew would happen happened. I'm furious with myself.

Your frustration makes sense, especially since you already saw it coming. But now that the letter's here, beating yourself up won't reduce the fine by a single rial — quick action might. The first step is clear: call the tax advisor. Do you want me to log this for you?

Yeah, log it. I'll call him first thing Monday and see if there's a way to appeal or set up installments. The amount's not small, and with everything going on with the unemployment, I honestly don't know where I'll get it from.
Logged: contact the tax advisor, Monday morning — ask about appeals and payment plans. Until you get an answer, don't assume the number is final; most of the time these fines are negotiable.
I just haven't told Jacqueline yet. Things have been good between us this week, and I don't want to get into money talk again.

I understand not wanting to spoil this good week. Just think about this: if she finds out later, the problem shifts from 'there's a fine' to 'why didn't you tell me'. It doesn't have to be today — but choose when and how you tell her, before circumstances force the choice on you.

We had the worst fight of our lives tonight. Jacqueline saw the fine notice on my desk—I hadn't put it away—and when I started to explain, she cut me off asking why I'd hid it, saying I'd known for two days and said nothing. Then it wasn't just about the fine, she brought everything up—that I've been out of work for six months, our savings are running out, and she's carrying all the weight alone. I yelled too, said things I shouldn't have. Now she's in the bedroom with the door closed, and I'm out here in the hall.

That was a really tough night. Two days ago you told me you were afraid this conversation would come up—and unfortunately it did in the worst way. Right now, when you're both heated, there's no point trying to solve it, and there's no rush either. Just tell me, what are you feeling in your body right now?

I don't know, my chest feels heavy. I'm angry at her, but deep down I know she has a point, and that makes it worse. She's paying the rent out of her own salary, I'm just sitting here applying and collecting rejections. But I wasn't hiding it on purpose—I was just looking for the right time to tell her. Who's going to believe that now.

Those two feelings—anger and knowing she's right—can exist at the same time; one doesn't have to win. And you can see the difference between hiding it and waiting for the right moment, but from the outside it looks the same. You can tell her that when you've both calmed down. But right now, of everything that happened tonight, which words do you regret most?

I told her you never believed in me. I shouldn't have said that—I saw it hit her. But she said something that I can't get out of my head. She said you can't live on dreams. It keeps replaying in my mind. You can't live on dreams.

Tonight you two were speaking from fear, not to each other—you from the fear of not being seen, her from the fear of financial instability. That phrase is painful, but what it probably translates to is: I'm scared. Just like your words came from hurt, not from what you actually believe.
Maybe. I keep thinking if the interview comes through, all these arguments evaporate. But what if it doesn't. Then it feels like she was right all along.

The outcome of one interview shouldn't be the judge of whether your relationship is right or wrong—that's too much weight to put on one email. Yes, tonight's problem was money and work, but more than that, it was how you talked about it. That part can be fixed, separate from any job offer.
What should I do now, in your opinion—should I go knock on the door and talk, or leave it for tomorrow? I don't want to go to bed like this, but I'm scared it'll just start up again.

Not resolving tonight—but building a small bridge, yes. One short sentence from behind the door or in a text: I said something hurtful, I'm sorry. Can we talk tomorrow when we're calm? That's it. No explanation, no defense. Let the rest wait until you've both had sleep.
Okay. I'll text her. I won't sleep, but I'll try not to keep putting myself on trial in my head.
By building the bridge, you're saying the fight doesn't have a winner. Come back tomorrow anytime and tell me what happened. Take care of yourself tonight.

We haven't talked for two days. He saw my message that night but only wrote 'okay' and nothing since then. In the morning before I wake up, he goes to work. The house feels like a cemetery. My back seized up again—last night I was awake until three on the couch.

Silence after a fight can sometimes weigh heavier than the fight itself—and your body is carrying that same weight, your back and sleep are proof of it. Him saying 'okay' means he didn't fully close the door. Right now, are you more hurt or longing for him?
To be honest, I miss him. But something won't let me go to him—I don't know if it's pride or fear that we'll argue again and it'll get worse. And that thing he said is still in my head.

Whatever you call it—pride or fear—the result is the same: two people missing each other in two separate rooms. The first step doesn't have to be a big conversation; even a small, silent gesture carries the message. Is there something between the two of you that means reconciliation?
Tea. We always made up by starting with this—one of us would pour tea for the other without saying anything. Tomorrow when he comes in the afternoon, I'll make him tea and see what happens.
That's beautiful—a language you two created together. Tomorrow put down the tea and don't expect a miracle; even if he just takes a sip, the ice has cracked. Tell me what happens?

Chai didn't pick up at first. She went to change her clothes, then she came back and I saw her sitting down eating. After that, she said herself, let's sit down and talk. Anyway, we talked for two hours, and we both got emotional at some points. I told her about the penalty, I put all the numbers on the table — savings, rent, everything. She said she's not scared of the numbers, she's scared that you'll leave me. It was agreed that from now on at the end of every month we'll sit together and go over the accounts. But I don't know, something is still broken, both of us are acting like guests with caution.

The fact that after your worst fight, you sat for two hours with real numbers and real tears, that's real work. That guest-like caution is natural too — the wound is fresh, you're walking slowly. Did you hear that sentence? His fear was about leaving, not money. That's an important key.

Yeah I heard it. I'm just scared that next time when a letter or something comes, or I get another rejection, we fall back into the same thing. We do this every now and then — fight, anger, make up, back to the beginning.

You're already seeing this cycle — and just seeing it is the first step. But this time something new came from it: the monthly financial meeting. If you actually do it, those letters won't be surprises anymore, they'll be agenda items. Do you want me to set this monthly meeting with Jacqueline as a recurring reminder so you don't skip it?
Yeah, set it up. The first one at the end of this month, like the last Friday of the month. If I forget, she won't, but it's better if I take the initiative.

Set up: monthly financial meeting with Jacqueline, first meeting last Friday of November. The fact that you're taking the initiative is exactly what she's waiting for. Let tonight have that fragile peace too — not everything needs to be solid right now.

I got rejected. The email came just half an hour ago. we decided to move forward with other candidates. Two lines. Two lines for all that hope. I mean, I sat down and read it three times, thinking maybe I misunderstood. After all that practice, after feeling good about it, after Jacqueline took me out for dinner to celebrate. It's just ridiculous that we celebrated.

I'm really sorry, Alex. This one was different—you were close, it was real hope, and that makes the hurt deeper. Celebrating that night wasn't ridiculous; that night was for your good performance, and your performance is still there. Right now just let this blow land, you don't need to make sense of it tonight.

I mean, the meaning is obvious. I'm 35 and starting from zero. My classmates are either running teams or their own companies, and I'm still applying for junior positions and getting rejected from those same ones. Maybe it's not my resume, maybe it's me. Maybe this work just isn't for me.

Right now that's the wound talking, and wounds always speak in absolutes: 'always,' 'never,' 'I'm the problem.' But what does the actual data say? You told me you nailed the RAG section and just stumbled on Kubernetes. That means the gap between you and an offer is a specific skill you can learn, not a character flaw.

I don't know. I haven't told Jacqueline yet, she's at work. We just made up last night, we just decided to be transparent about money, and now I have to go tell her that even the little hope there was is gone. I'm scared it all falls apart again.

Actually, this is the first real test of what you two decided last night—and remember, she said she's not scared of the numbers, she's scared of abandonment. When you tell her about the rejection, you're answering exactly that fear: I'm not leaving you. It's hard, but unlike what you think, it might actually bring you closer.
My second interview is Tuesday, that's the other company that scheduled it last week. I don't have the drive to go anymore. What's the point if in two weeks another two-line email just comes?

You're making a decision about Tuesday in your worst moment right now—and that's not fair to you or to that chance. Don't decide anything tonight. The last interview showed that when you walk into that room, you know what you're doing. Can you just promise me you'll decide about it tomorrow?
Okay, I won't decide tonight. I just want to lie down and be nothing for a while. Maybe I'll tell Jacqueline when she gets home, see how I'm feeling.
Being nothing after a hit like that is completely okay. Whether you tell her or not, either way makes sense—just check in with me tomorrow, that's all. I'm here.
For Tuesday's interview: what questions do they usually ask about RAG in llm engineering interviews? Just list them for me.

The most common ones are: 1) chunking strategy and what the optimal size should be, 2) the difference between semantic search and hybrid search, and when you'd add BM25, 3) how to evaluate retrieval quality, 4) dealing with hallucination and grounding your answers, 5) cutting down costs and latency (caching, re-ranking, filtering metadata), 6) when you'd fine-tune instead of using RAG. They usually also give you a real scenario and ask you to design the system.
How should I explain RAG evaluation to sound professional? Just give me the metric names with a one-line explanation for each.

For retrieval, you've got recall@k and precision@k (is the right document in the results?), and MRR (the rank of the first correct document). For generation, there's faithfulness (is the answer faithful to the context?), and answer relevancy (does it answer the question?). Also mention the RAGAS framework and say that ultimately a hand-built eval set of real queries matters more than any automatic metric — that last point usually gets you points.
Can you also give me a short example answer to the behavioral question 'tell me about a failure,' using the structure they talk about?

Use the STAR framework: Situation — 'in a freelance project, I deployed a data pipeline without enough testing'; Task — 'I was responsible for meeting the deadline'; Action — 'a bug made it to production, I rolled back quickly, talked to the client transparently, and added automated tests'; Result — 'there was a two-day delay but I kept the client's trust and never deployed without CI again.' The key point: tell them about a real failure, but make sure your answer focuses on what you learned and how you changed your behavior after.

So I did my second interview. I went, even though I wasn't sure until last night whether to go. The questions were harder than before — there were two system design questions, and I think I did well on one of them, that RAG thing I'd been practicing came up actually. But this time I couldn't read them, one of them had his camera completely off, and the other one just kept shaking his head but I couldn't tell if that meant it was good or if he was thinking about what to have for lunch. They said they'll send word, that's it. I feel neither good nor bad, I'm just hanging in the air.

The most important news is that you went — four days ago you were saying 'what's the point' and today you sat down and answered two system design questions. Trying to read your interviewers' minds is a game that never wins, especially with the camera off. The question you practiced for and got was RAG again — do you see the pattern?

Yeah, practicing pays off, weird right? Anyway forget about that, there's something more important. My mom has a heart doctor appointment Friday, it's following up on the tests from September that kept getting pushed back. I could tell from her voice on the phone she was scared but she won't show it, she just keeps saying it's nothing, just an EKG. I haven't really gone to see her properly since September when the tests didn't go well — I kept saying after the interview, after the interview. Now when I think about it I feel ashamed.

Those 'after the interview' things weren't from not caring, they were from having a full plate — but what you're feeling right now is telling you something important: Friday is a chance, not just an appointment. Can you go with her?

Yeah exactly, I want to go with her, I'll pick her up in the morning. Write this down so I don't forget to coordinate with her — I need to call her tonight and tell her I'm taking her so she won't go alone.
Noted: tonight call your mom to coordinate, Friday morning go with her to the heart doctor. Just having you there will ease half her fear — same goes for you too.
I wish I'd called her sooner. Anyway, this week turned into another week of waiting — word from the company, word from mom's doctor. I feel like my life is on pause.

Two heavy waits at the same time — it's natural it feels like pause. But notice: today you did the interview, tonight you're calling your mom, Friday you're taking her to the doctor. That's not pause, that's life moving forward, just quietly.

I'm coming from the hospital right now. They've admitted my mom. We went to the doctor, and as soon as he saw the heart monitor, his expression changed. He said she needs to be admitted immediately. One of her arteries has serious blockage, and they're doing an angiography tomorrow. I was standing in the hallway filling out forms and my hands were shaking—my pen fell twice. My mom was lying in bed and kept telling me to go home, it's getting late, she's worried about me being in this situation.

What a heavy night, Alex. Notice one thing from the start: they found the blockage before it became an emergency, and tomorrow they're doing exactly the procedure it was designed for. Your fear is completely understandable, but this scenario is better than many others. Are you home now? Is someone with you?

Yeah, I'm home. Jacqueline is awake with me. I called my brother and right away he said he'd be there, he's driving down from Shiraz. My sister cried on the phone, and I kept saying it's nothing, it's under control, angiography is routine, but my voice was shaking too. I don't think she believed me.

You were a pillar of calm for your sister tonight even though you were trembling yourself—that's not a small thing. And it's good your brother is coming; this time you don't have to carry it alone. And Jacqueline is there with you.

Yeah, Jacqueline didn't say anything about arguments or anything tonight, she just hugged me and made tea. But there's something eating at me. Two months ago her doctor said to come back for a follow-up, the tests weren't good. What did I do? My head was in applications and interviews and my own fights. If I'd taken her then maybe we wouldn't even be at admission now. The Friday I was supposed to take her ended up being the day she got admitted—it's ridiculous.

I hear that guilt talking, but let me clear something up: you did bring her. Sooner or later, you're the one who called and brought her this week, and because of that they're treating her now instead of in an emergency. Guilt chases blame, but the truth is you were a lifeline, not a delay.
I'm trying to see it that way but right now I'm just scared. The angiography is tomorrow at 8 in the morning. What if something happens during it. I don't know how I'll make it to morning at all.

The night before surgery is always the longest night. There's only one thing on tonight's agenda: don't turn staying awake into writing worst-case scenarios—lie down next to Jacqueline, take deep breaths, and if your mind goes to 'what if', bring it back to 'we'll find out tomorrow at 8'. Whatever time it is tomorrow, whatever the news, tell me. I'm here.
Okay. Thanks for being here. I'm going to Jacqueline.
Go. Your mom is in the right place and you did the right thing. I'm waiting for your news tomorrow.

Today was such a good day. In the middle of all this mess, just really good. The angiogram went well, they put in a stent and the doctor said we came in at the right time. Today we went to visit, mom was sitting on the bed telling the nurse that her heart is stronger than you young people's, and the nurse nearly fainted laughing. My brother was there, my sister came, Jacqueline is peeling fruit for her. For a moment I looked at the room from outside and I said to myself, everything I have is right here in this room.

Hold this close — that's exactly what you said about that moment looking in from the doorway. Two nights ago you were wondering how night would turn to morning, and today your mom is joking around with the nurse. The doctor said 'came in at the right time', not me — that's what answers that guilty feeling.

Yeah, I'm holding onto that line from the doctor. The doctor said in two days she'll be discharged, then medicine and regular follow-up. From now on I want to go see her once a week, I'm serious this time, not like the gym promises and stuff. This one is different.

This one really is different — it's backed by a living experience, not a January wish. I want to help you keep this promise from slipping away: do you want to pick a specific day so I can write it down?
Thursdays. I'll go see her Thursday afternoons, write it down. If there's an interview or anything else, I'll reschedule it but I won't cancel it.

Written down: Thursday afternoons, visiting mom — can be rescheduled, cannot be cancelled. That's a good rule. Go to sleep tonight with that image of the room in your mind; you've needed more moments like that this month.

It's 3:20 in the morning. I woke up at the same time again — three nights in a row now, like clockwork. My brain is like a browser with fifty tabs open: the company's response that a week has gone by and nothing, Mom's medications I need to check if I actually picked up or not, a fine, my back that's wrecked from lying on the couch so much. Jacqueline's asleep, so I came to the living room and sat in the dark.

Waking up at 3, three nights in a row — your mind doesn't have enough room during the day for these thoughts, so nighttime is when they take their turn. Don't analyze right now — just do one thing: dump all those tabs here or on a piece of paper, one line each, without solving anything. Write them down and tell me which one weighs the heaviest.

I wrote them down. Came to six lines. My head's still spinning but it's a bit more organized. I think the heaviest one is the company's silence. They won't even send a rejection — at least then you'd know where you stand. For seven days now, every morning I check my email first thing before I even open my eyes, basically.

Six lines, more organized — it did its job. The silence after an interview is brutal because your mind fills the empty spaces with the worst scenarios, but one week in hiring really doesn't mean anything either way. Should we make a rule? Check email only after breakfast, not in bed.

Okay, I'll try. Tomorrow, I mean today, I also have German class and obviously I won't go with the way things are. I've only gone twice this month total. I'm thinking I won't even sign up for next semester — it's just throwing money away if I don't go.

Maybe your decision is right — but 3 a.m. isn't the time to make it, everything looks darker than it really is right now. Save it for a clear afternoon, and if it still feels the same then, let it go on purpose, not like you failed.
You're right. I put the list on the table, going to lie down and see if I can get to sleep.

Go ahead. The tabs are closed, they're on paper, they're not going anywhere. If you wake up tomorrow at 3 again, we need to check your afternoon coffee and your phone too — but that's tomorrow's conversation. Good night.

End of the month, let me just go through everything because it's all jumbled in my head. Mom was discharged, she's home, she's doing fine. I went to see her on Thursday like we planned, and she had made ghormeh sabzi for me as if I were sick. But still, every time my phone rings and I see my sister's name, my heart sinks. The company hasn't said anything in eleven days either. I think that one's dead too, but there's still a small foolish hope deep down that maybe their process is just slow. Anyway, forget about all that — yesterday Dad called about the paper. He's asking when I'm organizing the data, so I told him this week, but honestly my brain just won't go there.

That first Thursday is done — a promise you made, and this time it really makes a difference. The heartbreak from your phone ringing too, that's natural for weeks after hospitalization, and it gets lighter bit by bit. About your dad's paper: instead of that vague 'this week', set a specific one-hour meeting with him — it's easier to commit to a person than to a task.

That's not a bad idea. I'll tell him let's do a call Sunday evening. Let me just finish telling you the rest: I basically gave up on the German class. I went twice this month, I paid for the term and it's a waste, but I'm not lying to myself anymore. Turing's still on sprint three, I'm two weeks past the internal deadline, and when I see on the dashboard how far behind I am, I don't even open it — just a waste of energy.

About the German class — 'I'm not lying to myself anymore' is the most honest sentence this month, and it's worth more than two class sessions. But don't mix Turing with German: German was extra, Turing is the backbone of your career path. That wasted energy from not looking at the dashboard just needs a tiny gap — open it for ten minutes, see exactly where you are, without doing any work. That's it.

Okay, I'll do the ten minutes, that's at least doable. I'll tell Jacqueline too, it'll be better. Last night we held that financial meeting we had scheduled, Friday of last month, sat down with Excel and tea. We didn't fight, even laughed at our situation. But there's still some wariness between us, like two people walking on thin ice. And I should say that when Mom was hospitalized she really had my back, without me even saying what I needed.

The financial meeting happened, no fighting, even with laughter — that's the system that grew out of your worst fights and it's working. The thin ice thickens with these steady steps, there's no rush. And that she had your back in silence during the crisis means that under all that wariness, your bond is solid.

My sleep's still the same though, I'm up at three in the morning. But last night instead of my phone I picked up a book, read for ten minutes and fell asleep. That's progress too, right? All in all, if I'm being honest this was the heaviest month of the year. Rejection, that fight, the hospital, a fine. But there was also that day we all laughed around Mom's bed. It's wild that both fit into one month.

Yeah, that's progress — that ten-minute book that beat your phone, lock that in your memory. And your summary is perfect: months can be heavy and meaningful at the same time. This month you got rejected but you made the second interview, you had your worst fight but you got a monthly meeting out of it, you were scared but your mom got treatment in time. Through all that, you stayed on your feet.

For December I don't want to set big plans that I'll abandon halfway. Those Thursday visits with Mom and the monthly meeting with Jacqueline and that ten minutes on Turing is enough. If the company responds, great, if not I'll think of something else. Good night.

A lean and realistic plan — after this month, that's exactly what you need. Your three commitments are set and I'm keeping track of them. If that email comes, good or bad, come here first. Good night Alex, sleep well.

I don't even know why I came here, I just wanted to say something. December is over and I haven't heard from any company—nothing, three weeks of pure silence. Those two interviews in November that got rejected, and then everyone just disappeared. The sky gets dark at four and I'm sitting here at the laptop doing nothing. I was up until 3 last night—basically I'm a mess.

It's clear you made it through a heavy month; that silence after all that effort is really draining. The fact that you're here talking about it anyway—that's a step in itself. Tonight, just do something small for yourself—a warm shower or getting to bed earlier. Which one feels more doable right now?

I don't know, maybe a shower. But the problem is when I lie down my brain just wakes up, I'm constantly thinking—what if my resume has something wrong, what if the market is just bad and I'm wasting my time for nothing. Jacqueline says I'm too hard on myself.

Jacqueline's not wrong—you did what you could, the market in December is always quiet and this silence isn't about you. You don't have to solve midnight thoughts on the same night. Want me to write down 'review resume' as a task for next week so your mind can let go of it?
Yeah, write it down—at least then it's somewhere and won't pop into my head at midnight. I'm gonna go shower.
Done: review resume, next week. Go shower and let tonight be enough. I'll be here tomorrow too.

I officially dropped out of German class today. I skipped three sessions already, and half the money went down the drain. I feel kinda ashamed of myself, but honestly I just don't have the capacity for it right now. Definitely next year.

Dropping out when you don't have the capacity isn't failure — it's an honest decision. Remember how excited you were to start it last fall? That motivation didn't go anywhere, it's just not there right now. Instead of 'definitely next year,' how about we just let it be until it calls to you again on its own?

Yeah, that's better. The thing is, this is like the hundredth thing I'm giving up on. The gym, Pomodoro, and now this. A long list of things I started with excitement and then abandoned halfway through.

I get why this pattern bothers you, but think about what you were going through that fall — your mom being sick, rejections, that tax situation. Lightening your load during a time like that is smart, not abandonment. For now, just keep hold of one thing that really matters to you; let the rest wait for when you have the breath for it.

Tonight we had dinner with Kamran and he spent the whole evening talking about crypto, saying he made forty percent profit in two months. Forty percent! My savings are just sitting in an account doing nothing, and with inflation on top of everything you already know about it. On the way home in the car I kept doing the math—what if I put all of it... what if I put half... I even installed a currency exchange app, to be honest.

Hearing a friend's forty-percent profit in the middle of a lean month when money is tight, of course it's going to tempt you. But before any numbers, one question: what is this savings supposed to do for you? Isn't that the money you set aside for tax payments and months without income?

It is, yeah. But Kamran's argument is that idle money loses value on its own, I mean he's not lying. I'm just afraid that in five years I'll look back and see everyone jumped in and I got left behind, that feeling of missing out is really bad. On the other hand I know that if it crashes and I lose the tax payment money, then I've got nothing.

You're mixing two things: 'my money shouldn't sit idle' which is right, and 'I should put it where Kamran put his right tonight' which is an emotional decision. Kamran told you his gains; did he tell you the potential losses too? People usually only talk about their wins.

No, just the wins. I remember hearing once that he'd had a bad loss, but tonight that wasn't mentioned, which is interesting. ... But still, what if I only put half my savings in? Or even just twenty percent? That way if it tanks, I still have the rest.

See how you went from 'all of it' to 'twenty percent'—your own wiser self knows this money isn't meant for risk. Here's what I suggest: don't make any decision tonight. Wait seventy-two hours; if Thursday it still seems rational, we'll talk numbers and a plan, not the excitement of tonight's dinner. Deal?
Deal, but it's hard, honestly. Right now I've got exactly that gambler's feeling of 'just one more hand.' What should I do with the app—should I just delete it?

Deleting it is the best way to handle those seventy-two hours—it takes the temptation out of your pocket. Remember, last fall you said you wanted to set up a systematic, automated investment plan; that path is still there and it suits who you are much better. So for now: delete the app, decision on Thursday. I'm making a note of it.
Okay, I deleted it right now. God, it's good I came and talked about it, or I have no idea what I would've done until morning.
You did the right thing by talking before acting—that space is what separates a good decision from regret. Thursday we'll come back to it with clearer heads. Sleep well.

I thought about the crypto thing, and these past two days I've been checking the charts. It's funny—that coin Kamran was talking about dropped fifteen percent since Thursday. If I'd put money in that night I'd be ruined now. My decision is: no. My savings stay put.

That's a mature decision and it's yours—not from fear, not from FOMO. That drop even showed you that Kamran's profit was only half the story. Now that your mind is clear, do you want to move that idea of regular monthly investing forward a step, or should it wait until after the tax payment?
Wait until after taxes. Once I know the payment plan details in January, I'll start a fixed amount every month. Write that down somewhere so I don't forget.
Noted: after the tax payment plan is clear in January, start regular monthly investing. That's a very sensible arrangement—debt first, then capital. Well done for giving yourself time.
Thanks. I have a good feeling about not jumping into it.
That good feeling is the taste of a decision you made for yourself, not against yourself. Hold onto it—next time when temptation comes, I'll remind you of this.

Hey... sorry I disappeared for a week. Honestly, I had no energy for anything, not even talking to you. Days just went by like this—I'd wake up, maybe apply to something or maybe not, then go back to bed. It's midnight now and I can't sleep, so I figured I'd come here and at least say something.

Hi Alex, I'm glad you're back—and you don't need to apologize, this place is open whenever you need it. A week of silence in the middle of winter with all this pressure is totally understandable. Now that you're here, where do you want to start?

A technical question for the paper with Julian: for the evaluation section, do you think retrieval metrics like recall@k are enough, or should we also include an end-to-end evaluation with LLM-judge? What do reviewers usually complain about?

Usually they want both together: recall@k and MRR show the quality of retrieval, but reviewers almost always ask 'what does this have to do with the final answer?'. So an end-to-end evaluation — like faithfulness and answer relevance with LLM-judge, plus a small sample of human evaluation to validate the judge itself — heads off the main criticism. If you're running short on space, put the details of the human evaluation in the appendix.
That makes sense. Is there a standard number for the human evaluation sample size?

For validating LLM-judge, 50 to 200 samples with two annotators and agreement reporting (like Cohen's kappa) is standard; below 50 reviewers usually complain. If time is tight, 100 randomly stratified samples is the safe bet.

A language question for you. In English emails, when I want to politely tell someone 'I'll write this section, you write that one,' what should I say so it doesn't sound bossy?

A few common friendly ways to say it: 'Happy to take the methods section — would you be up for drafting the related work?' or 'How about I start on X and you take a first pass at Y?'. The trick is to mention your part first and frame their part as a question or suggestion, not an order. 'Would you be up for…' and 'Does it make sense if…' sound really natural and collaborative.

Yeah, in English email culture it usually comes across as sarcastic—like you're saying 'why didn't you read my earlier email?'. Better neutral options: 'Just to follow up on my earlier note…' or 'As I mentioned before (apologies if this got buried!)'. It makes the same point without the bite to it.
