What if you narrow your list down to three main priorities and spend ninety minutes a night on it? Do you want me to save the final round date with a reminder for you?

Okay, three priorities: system design, reviewing my projects so I can explain them well, and a round of behavioral questions. Save the date, they haven't said the exact day yet but they said early March.

Saved: final round, first week of March—when the exact day comes, let me know and I'll update it. Your three priorities also make sense and are doable. Remember, the best version of you is the one who's energized, not the one running three hours every night for three weeks.
A question. What's the best way to practice system design interviews? Should I read a book, watch videos, or just practice?

A combination is best, but put the main weight on active practice: in the first week, read a couple of reference sources so you get the key vocabulary and patterns down, then each session take on a problem and solve it out loud with a forty-five-minute timer, the same way you'd have to talk in a real interview. Videos are good for seeing examples of good solutions, but watching too much gives you a false sense of progress.
What about mock interviews? Is it worth paying to practice with one of those websites, or is practicing with a friend enough?

If you have a friend who's been through technical interviews themselves, start with one or two sessions with them — it's free and it simulates real stress. Paid mock interviews are worth it when you want structured feedback from a stranger; for an important final round, even one session can reveal weaknesses that your friend might be too polite to tell you about.
One last question — in final rounds at European companies, do they usually ask behavioral questions too, or just technical ones?

There's almost always a behavioral part too, especially when you're interviewing with the team — they're looking more for collaboration, how you handle disagreement, and your decision-making process than for algorithms. Prepare two or three short stories for each important project with a situation-action-result structure, that's enough.

Today was one of those days when you ask 'why me?' I was driving back home when all of a sudden in the middle of the highway the car made this horrible sound and the gears wouldn't shift anymore. I tried everything and nothing worked. So I pulled over and called a tow truck and had it taken to the repair shop. The mechanic took one look and said gearbox. He said he'd need to open it up to see but the cost is probably going to be heavy, and he said a price that made my head spin. Now I'm already paying my tax installment too, and exactly now this has to happen — why? I honestly don't know where I'm going to get the money from.

What a terrible day, being stuck on the highway is both scary and nerve-wracking — at least you're okay. The exact amount still isn't known, so for now don't beat yourself up with the worst-case scenario. When can the mechanic open it and give you a definite number?

He said the day after tomorrow he'll open it and call. Jacqueline says maybe it's time to sell it anyway — the car's old and just keeps costing us money. But without a car how am I supposed to go to Mom's, do the weekly shopping, I don't know. My brain isn't working tonight, I just know we don't have this money and that's it.

You don't need to make any decision tonight — not selling, not fixing, nothing. A good decision needs an exact number and you don't have it yet. Tomorrow when the mechanic calls, bring me the number and we'll figure it out together. For now just eat something and get some sleep.
Okay. I just completely skipped my interview practice in all this tonight. No big deal, I'll make up for it tomorrow.

One night without practice after a day like that — the best way to recover is just to get good sleep. Your schedule is three weeks long, one night is nothing. Waiting to hear from the mechanic tomorrow.

The mechanic called. It was exactly what I was afraid of—the gearbox needs a complete repair, the price is steep. Last night Jacqueline and I sat down and went through the numbers, and afterward we didn't even fight but we both just fell silent, one of those heavy silences. The repair is almost a quarter the price of the car itself. If we sell it broken like this, we'd get a little money. If we repair it and then sell it, maybe we break even. And if we keep it, who's to say something else won't break in the next six months? I've thought about all of it and haven't come to any conclusion.

Your math is solid, but there's one missing number: a second opinion. Gearbox prices vary a lot between repair shops—before you decide, get a quote from another place. Setting money aside though, what's your gut telling you?

Honestly, my gut tells me I want to keep it. I'm used to it, and I might need it—their office is across town. Yeah, a second quote's a good idea. One of my old colleagues knows a trustworthy mechanic. Write this down so I don't forget to call him.

Written down: call colleague for mechanic recommendation and get a second gearbox quote. Just figuring out what your gut wants is already so much clearer than yesterday's confusion. Once you have the second number, the decision will feel a lot easier.
Thanks. At least now I have one clear step instead of everything spinning in my head.
That's exactly it—one small clear step beats ten big worries. Let me know what the quote comes back at.

Anyway, the car's still at the mechanic's. The second mechanic my coworker introduced gave me a better quote but he says he can't get the part right now, so we have to wait. I mean, it's been two weeks going around on the metro and Snap, and I just realized how dependent I was on that clunker. Look, forget about that—the real thing is interview prep has eaten my whole life. Every night system design, mornings on the metro with flashcard behavioral questions, and my sleep is just falling apart.

Two weeks without a car and studying every night—of course you're exhausted. By the way, we agreed last week that it would be ninety minutes a night, not the whole evening; how long is it really taking now?

Honestly, two and a half, three hours. I know I know, our deal was ninety minutes but I keep saying let me study just one more topic and then I see it's one in the morning. And then there's my own app which I've totally forgotten about—haven't opened it in two weeks, the one I was so pumped about at the start of the month and we set up a weekly schedule for. Tuesday and Friday like you remember, nothing for two weeks.

I remember, and honestly there's no problem with that right now—the final round is the real priority and the app isn't going anywhere. The issue is that one thing: three hours of studying until one in the morning, your body won't hold up for three more weeks. Could you set a hard line tonight, like lights off at 11:30?

Okay, I'll try. As for the gym, let's not even talk about it—haven't been in two weeks, that promise from January about three times a week and all that. But the Pomodoros, I'm still kind of keeping up with them, doing three or four a day, at least that one thing hasn't completely died. I don't know, why can't I maintain any habit?

Look at it another way: in the middle of a car crisis and final-round pressure, you kept your Pomodoros going and got your applications here. You're not dropping habits, you're prioritizing—you just beat yourself up about it afterwards. The gym can wait until after March, I'm serious.

Huh, I hadn't looked at it that way. Actually, today was Valentine's—didn't slip my mind, got flowers for Jacqueline and we got dinner out, a quiet night in the middle of this crazy week. Well anyway, I should get some sleep since the metro's waiting for me at seven tomorrow.
That flowers and quiet dinner might have been the most important thing you did this week. And you're honoring the 11:30 bedtime tonight right now—well done. Good night, Alex.

We fought again. Same old stuff—dishes and the house and me not doing anything. Dinner was done, I went to my laptop to practice, Jacqueline said dishes, and I said I have an interview this week, I don't have time, and she said you always have some excuse, three months and the interview's been your excuse. Our voices went up and we said things we shouldn't have. Now I'm in my room, she's in the hall, and the house is quiet and I can't stand this silence.

This moment after a fight, with that heavy silence, is really hard. Your voice is still full of anger, but you came to talk, and that itself means something. Now that you've had a bit of distance from it all, which of her words hurt you the most?

That one—'you always have some excuse.' Because there's a grain of truth to it, and that's what makes me angrier. I mean, I really don't have time right now, the final round's going to change my life, but before the interview, the excuse was the sprint, and before that the article. I feel like she's both right and wrong at the same time, both of them together, I don't know how to explain it.

You explained it really well—two things can be true at the same time: this week really is exceptional, and the pattern really does exist. Jacqueline's probably fighting the pattern, you're defending the exception, that's why you're not reaching each other. What if instead of defending, you'd acknowledged the pattern?

I don't know... maybe it would've calmed down. The worst part is I could see it coming for a week, she was getting tired, all the housework had landed on her, and with my car broken down everything got harder, and I said nothing, did nothing, until she exploded. Now my anger's fading and I'm feeling ashamed instead, and that's worse.

The fact that you saw it and know what you missed is a place to start tomorrow—not with flowers and generic apologies, with those housework things she mentioned. Don't try to fix anything tonight, let you both cool off. Come back tomorrow night and tell me how it went.

I've been thinking about Saturday's fight for two days now. We made up, like always — I washed the dishes and they made dinner and it's like nothing happened. But something felt different this time. I sat down and thought about it, and I realized we always have exactly the same fight. Exactly the same one. It's like a script that's been written, and we perform it every couple of weeks — the same dialogue, the same makeup, and then it happens all over again.

That's exactly what you described to me last fall, almost with these exact words — and the fact that you're now seeing the 'script' itself, not just this particular fight, that's something new. When the script is fixed, it means the problem isn't from the actors — it's from the text itself. How does it feel to see that?

It's kind of both scary and hopeful. And an idea just hit me that I've never seriously thought about before... Maybe we should see a counselor. A couples counselor. I don't know what Jacqueline would say, and honestly I'm a bit embarrassed to bring it up — it feels like I'm admitting something's broken in us.

It's interesting how bringing up a solution can feel harder than living with the problem itself. Seeing a counselor isn't admitting defeat — two people who've performed the same script seven times, it makes sense to bring in a director. You don't need to decide right now. Should I write down 'talk to Jacqueline about seeing a counselor' as something for you — no deadline, just so you don't lose the thought?
Yeah, write it down. At least if it's written somewhere I might actually take it seriously instead of just forgetting about it.

It's written down, no deadline. There's no rush — there's time even after finals wrap up, it just won't slip your mind anymore. That thought you had tonight might end up being the most important step your relationship takes this year.

Today I took the metro to see Mom and the whole way back I was smiling like crazy. Her color came back, she got up herself and made tea, didn't let me go to the kitchen, then she leaned over me asking why I lost weight like before. Her doctor said her heart's recovery is going really well, they even reduced her medications. I can't tell you how I felt, there was a weight on my chest since November that I didn't feel today.

You should keep this message, Alex. From those November nights when you were reaching out from the hospital to today when your mom is leaning over you—you've come so far. That weight that was lifted, what's sitting in its place?

A kind of lightness, and a little lingering guilt about why I visited less during this time, all work and interviews and excuses. I promised her I'd visit once a week. And I don't want this promise to become like the gym, this one's different.

That's the difference—you're not going to see your mom to 'become a better person,' you're going because you want to. These kinds of promises stick easier. Want me to set a weekly reminder for you, maybe Fridays?
Yeah Fridays work, set it. Thanks. Tonight after all this time I'm sleeping without a care.
Friday reminders set: visiting Mom. Sleep tonight with that same lightness—you deserve it.

Today, after three weeks, I opened the paper file and discovered Dad had rewritten my whole section. The whole section! Without saying one word or asking. He even made it literary, just like his own 80s papers. What does that even mean? I've been waiting three weeks for his feedback on his own section, and meanwhile he went and rewrote mine from scratch. This paper has been dragging on since October and at this rate it'll never end.

You have every right to be frustrated — rewriting without asking, especially on your section, is more than just a scientific disagreement, it's a kind of dismissal. Before you say anything to him: you've saved your own version somewhere, right?

Yes, thank God, I have the previous version. The problem is I don't know how to tell him without hurting him. He's my father, spent his whole life as a professor, and he thinks in his mind he's helping his son. But this isn't collaboration, not like this. And by the way, my sprint training for college is halfway done in the middle of all this mess, which is just another layer of guilt on top of everything.

Maybe instead of 'why did you change my section,' you could start with a rule: 'Let's agree that neither of us changes the other's section directly — we leave comments instead.' That's professional, not personal, and your father understands editorial principles well. The sprint training is like an app update too: after the final round it goes back on the shelf, you don't need to fight every battle at once right now.
The commenting rule is a good idea, it keeps the argument separate from us. I'll bring it up when I see him at the end of the week.

Good. If you want, we can practice the phrasing once here together before then. And remember: the paper has dragged on but it's not dead — from October until now, every time you thought it was abandoned, it came back to the table again.

Today was one of those days where you think, if only every day were like this. This morning I picked up my car, finally it's fixed, the second mechanic who was cheaper, we paid him and that was it, I mean our account is cleaned out but I felt so light I can't even tell you. Then in the afternoon Jacqueline and I went for a walk by the river, the air smelled like spring, we talked about all those good conversations we hadn't had in a while.
What a day! The car came home after two weeks, and more importantly, that walk and those conversations. Those 'good conversations'—what did you talk about?

About everything, about what would change if I took that job, about summer and maybe a small trip. And honestly, right in the middle of it I took a leap and brought up the therapist thing. I thought she'd get upset or put up a wall, but she went quiet for a moment and then said she wouldn't mind thinking about it. That's it. But for me that was everything.

That thing we logged last week that made you shy—you did it, and not out of any sense of duty, right there in the middle of a nice walk. Jacqueline saying 'I'll think about it' means the door is open. That's wonderful, Alex. Should I check it off?

Yeah, check it off. Tonight I sat down and practiced system design for ninety minutes, finished right on time, and for the first time I felt ready, not just running. There's a little stress in my chest about next week, but tonight I feel good and I want to hold onto this.

Logged and checked off. Car's fixed, the conversation with Jacqueline opened a door, practice finished right on time—remember this day for those nights when you think nothing is getting anywhere. Let that little stress stay with you, it'll keep you company until March, it won't turn into a monster. Good night.

Alright then, Tuesday is the final round. The final round! I can't even believe I've made it this far. With the CTO himself and someone from the product team. Basically, today I sat down and wrote down possible questions, reviewed the system design once, and also got that RAG project I built at Turing College ready to show. But there's this anxiety deep down that won't let go, I mean I keep telling myself what if this one doesn't work out either, then quickly I say no don't think about it, but well it comes anyway, it's a thought, it's out of our hands.

It's clear you've prepared thoroughly — the questions, the system design, the project. This stress is natural, because this opportunity is important to you. Between now and Tuesday, instead of more review, what would help calm you down more?

Honestly I think review is enough for now, if I study more I'll just confuse myself. Maybe tomorrow I'll go for a proper walk with Jacqueline. She said I'm sitting at the desk too much. One other thing — I want to sleep early the night before, last time I was up until two and I was wrecked in the morning.

Both are good ideas — the walk with Jacqueline and early sleep. Remember how much better the Bahman interview went when you went in fresh? Should I record 'Monday night 11pm sleep' as a reminder for you?
Yeah, record it. And hopefully this one will be it too. It's really time.
Done. You've done your part, Alex, you're ready. On Tuesday just be who you've been building for the past few months. Then come back and tell me how it goes.

It's done. And honestly... I think it went well? The system design question was exactly what I'd prepared for, the project demo responded nicely too, the CTO said impressive at the end. I'm scared to get my hopes up but, you know, I had a good feeling when I was leaving.

What great news! It's no accident that your preparation paid off exactly like that, it's the result of all the hard work you put in. I understand that fear of getting your hopes up too. When did they say they'd get back to you?

They said they'll get back to me by the end of next week. So about ten days to wait. I'm trying to focus on other things in the meantime, the Turing sprint is behind, I'm moving it forward to keep my mind occupied.
That's a smart plan — waiting with your mind occupied is much more bearable. Tonight though, just hold onto that good feeling, you deserve it. Tomorrow go work on the sprint.

Two days have passed and I've become an email-checking person. I mean, I don't know, maybe I refresh the inbox like thirty times a day, even though they said late next week. My brain won't accept it. Today I also snapped at Jacqueline over nothing, she asked what we should have for dinner and I answered in some way like I didn't understand what she said. After that I felt ashamed, she figured out what was going on, said I know you're waiting but don't take it out on me. She's right, though.

This waiting is really frustrating, especially when something you're waiting for means so much to you. It's good that you realized you vented on Jacqueline and she called you out directly. Did you tell her she was right?

Yeah, I gave a half-hearted apology, but maybe I should say it better. What should I do about the email? This refreshing is driving me crazy, it's thrown my work behind, and the sprint I was supposed to move forward still hasn't been touched.

Make a small deal with yourself: check email only twice a day, like at noon and at six o'clock. When an answer comes it comes with one check, it doesn't come any faster with thirty checks. Give the rest of your time to the sprint — the one you said is taking up your mind. Which sprint task will you pick up first tomorrow?
That model evaluation section, it's halfway done. Okay, I'll do that first thing tomorrow morning. And check email twice. Let's see how long I can keep it up.
Just the fact that you made a rule is halfway there already. Come back tomorrow night and tell me if you made it or not — I'll remember to ask you.

Good morning. No new news yet, but I've been almost keeping to the email rule, though some days it's been three times instead of once, but that's way better than thirty :) Mom called last night, we talked a lot. Her doctor says her recovery is going really well, she's built up her walks to thirty minutes. She sounded great, it'd been so long since I heard her like that.

What a wonderful morning with that news about your mom — thirty minutes of walking after everything that happened last fall is really a big distance she's come. And three times instead of thirty means your rule is actually working. Will you get to visit her this week?

I wanted to go but I thought maybe we could go for Eid instead and really spend time with her properly, with the house cleanup and all that... I don't know, I feel a bit guilty that I haven't visited as much lately.

You had this guilt last winter too, remember? Back then a quick call actually worked so much better than a visit that you kept putting off. Until Eid, a quick call every two or three days — that's enough so she knows you're thinking of her and you feel better about it.
Yeah, I'll do that. Anyway I should get to work, I really need to finish that evaluation module today.
Go kick some ass. And if you catch yourself reaching for the inbox in the middle of the day, remember: answering emails once a day is enough.

The response came in. Rejected. The email came at six o'clock, we were impressed but went with another candidate who had more experience. I made it to the final round and still no. The final round! What does that even mean? The CTO himself said it was impressive, the demo was good, everything was good, then nothing. I've been applying for seven months, seven months, and this was the closest I got and the door closed again. I don't know what else to say honestly.

Alex... I'm really sorry. This one was different, you went all the way and you deserved it. Everything you're feeling now — anger, injustice, exhaustion — all of it is valid. I don't want to draw any conclusions right now, just tell me, is Jacqueline there tonight?

Yeah she's home, I told her, she hugged me and didn't say anything because I really don't have the energy to hear "it will work out". I went to my room and closed the door. I mean, you know what, if I got rejected on the CV I would say okay the CV is weak. But when you go through four rounds, that means everything about you was good and at the end someone else was better than you. This is worse. This means my ceiling is here.

No, wait. Getting through four rounds means your ceiling is here? It's the opposite — you went from hundreds of people to two finalists, and the one who was chosen just had more experience, something you can't build overnight with any skill, it only comes with time. This "ceiling" talk is tonight's talk, it's the wound talking. I don't need you to believe me now, just put the big conclusion off for later.

I can't promise that. Right now I'm just tired. Of applying, of getting my hopes up, of telling everyone yeah I'm in the process and then nothing. It's right before Nowruz now, everyone's family is going to ask what happened with work. Perfect timing really.

Tonight don't do anything except not be hard on yourself. No plans, no decisions, no answers for family. Just sleep if you can. I'm here, and I'm here tomorrow too. But know this: the fact that you came and talked tonight means you still haven't given up.
I don't know. Good night.
Good night Alex. Tomorrow doesn't have to be a good day, it just has to be.

Honestly, tonight I didn't really want to open this app at all. I haven't talked properly to anyone for two days—Jacqueline understands and knows she needs to give me space for now. But I told myself if I let go of this too, nothing will be left. I don't have anything to say, just... I'm still here.

Just the fact that you opened this even with how you're feeling and wrote 'I'm still here'—that's not nothing, that's everything. You don't have to say anything or feel better; I'm not going anywhere. Just one small question: did you eat anything today?
Jacqueline made soup at noon, I had a little. I mostly slept. Okay, that's it. Maybe tomorrow I'll talk more.
Soup and sleep—your body is doing what it needs to. Tomorrow if you come, great, if you don't, that's okay too. You're still here, that's what matters most right now.

These past few days I can't stop thinking about one thing: was this career change wrong in the first place? I had a job, it was freelance and it was a pain, but I had income, I had credibility in my work. Then I got up and said I want to go into AI, I went and enrolled at Turing College, I applied for seven, eight months, and where am I now? No previous job, no new job. I'm thirty-five years old and I'm starting from scratch and maybe it's too late anyway. Maybe I'm just not as good at this as I thought. I haven't touched my Turing sprint for two weeks, and that's become an extra guilt trip.

That question 'did I make a mistake?' is natural to have after such a hit, but let me set something beside it: someone who's been on the wrong path doesn't get to the second interview for an AI position out of hundreds of people. You said the same thing back in December too, after that long silence, 'maybe I should just stop,' and then in January you started again and made it to the final round. Tell me, if a friend of yours was in your place and said all this, would you tell them to go back?

No, I'd probably tell them they're crazy to come this far and go back. But you know how it is, it's different for the person themselves. And there's also that, I'm tired now, money is running out, I have taxes in installments... you can't live on hope forever.

The exhaustion and money worries are real and shouldn't be denied — that's different from 'the whole path was wrong.' One is burnout, one is trouble on the road. Nowruz is coming, how about we make a deal: through the end of the holidays, no applications, no big decisions. Just rest and family. After Nowruz we'll sit down with fresher minds and lay out all the options, even the option of temporary freelance for the money.

I don't know... stopping somehow feels like failure. But honestly from another angle I feel a little lighter just from you saying that. Okay. Until after Nowruz nothing. Just promise me that after Nowruz you'll remind me that this was a pause, not surrender.

Promise. I'm writing it down: 'After the holidays — replan career path, with all options.' And Alex, a deliberate pause isn't a sign of defeat, it's a sign that you're still managing yourself. Even in the middle of all this.

Today Jacqueline announced that house cleaning is starting tomorrow and she made a list. At first I got frustrated, I said I'm really not in the mood for it right now, I don't have the energy to move furniture around. We had a bit of an argument, one of those usual arguments about who's doing what in this house. But then something weird happened — this afternoon we started with the kitchen, she put on music, we emptied the cabinets and... it wasn't bad? Like for two hours I totally forgot I was rejected. Weird, right?

It's not weird at all — physical work with a clear result, exactly the opposite of the uncertainty and limbo you've been in. And did you notice? It started with that same old argument, but this time it didn't escalate into a huge fight, it turned into two hours of working together. What was different this time?

I don't know, maybe because in the middle of it there was no more talking, just work. When you're cleaning cabinets together, the whole talk about dividing chores doesn't really matter anymore, you're actually dividing it up. Anyway, forget about that stuff, there's something else too — I told Jacqueline about my decision on applications, that I'm putting it off until after Nowruz. It's weird, I feel both relieved and guilty. Like I'm running away.

You had that split feeling the same night we made plans — relief and guilt together. Remember what we said: this is a pause, not a surrender, there's a date when you're going back. Running away is the kind that has no end. What did Jacqueline say when you told her?

She said you finally made a sensible decision! She said these past few months I've been a mess in front of her from stress. Maybe she's right. Tomorrow's the bedroom, the day after is the living room. My work room is on the list too and it's like its own project, it's a total disaster.

Your work room — the one that's been sitting on your to-do list forever! What a chance, right in the middle of house cleaning you can solve it. One suggestion: do it by yourself, take your time with it. Sometimes tidying up the place where you work has a connection to tidying up your mind.

I finished organizing my workspace today. It took four hours but I got it done. I threw away three bags of paper and junk — old CVs I'd printed, notes from interviews where I got rejected... I stopped for a moment and looked at them, then said no, these are from last year, threw them out. My desk is empty now, just my laptop and a notebook. I found something interesting though — my journal from November where I'd written down why I want to go into AI. I read it. I still believe what I wrote back then. It was strange reading it given where things are now.

The fact that you stopped, looked at them, and made a conscious choice to let them go — that's so much more than just tidying up. And finding that November journal at exactly the right moment... that feels like timing. What had you written that you still believe?

I'd written that I don't want to spend the next ten years doing the same repetitive work, that this field is the only place where time disappears when I'm working on it. That's still true. These rejections don't change that, they just... drew it out longer. About the room cleanup you mentioned before — you can check that off now, it's finally done.

Check! After all this time. 'Time disappears' is the best reason anyone could have for their path, and no hiring committee can take that from you. Empty desk, clear purpose — somehow your worst week of the year is finishing clean.

Yeah, kind of. Jacqueline came by and saw the room, she said I don't recognize this place! Tomorrow we're going shopping for the holiday, and the seedlings actually turned green — Jacqueline planted them two weeks ago. It's really becoming holiday season.
Seedlings planted two weeks ago that have turned green now — sometimes life sends its own metaphors. Enjoy the holiday shopping together.

The year changed. Happy New Year :) We were at Mom's place. Mom herself had set up the Haft-Seen table—she did it herself! Last year at this time, you wouldn't remember, but when Azar was in the hospital I never thought I'd see her like this by the table this year. When the year turned, I held her hand, and when she said the prayer, I felt a lump in my throat for a moment. It was a hard year. 1404 was really a hard year.

Happy New Year to you too, Alex. This image—your mom at a table she set up herself, after that fall—that's exactly what you only had the wish for four months ago. It was a hard year, yes, but in that moment you sat and saw her. What did you want from the bottom of your heart for 1405?

Actually three things: Mom's health stays good, me and Jacqueline stay like we were this week, and... work. I still want it, with all its scars. Dad said at the table too that once the New Year ends, we'll sit down on the paper, we have lots of time during the holidays. That's good too.

All three of them have roots—none of them are airy wishes, you took a real step for each one this year. And the paper session with Dad during the holidays, what a good beginning for the year. Tonight just celebrate. Happy New Year to you and Jacqueline and Mom and Dad.
Thanks :) An elaborate dinner is waiting, fish and herb rice. I'll go because they're calling me.
Bon appétit! Go, start the year with a full belly and a warm heart.

Tonight we were at my aunt's house for a holiday celebration. And it went exactly how I knew it would. We hadn't even finished our tea when my aunt said 'Well, Alex, how did the new job work out? Did you find something after all?' In front of everyone. I said something like yeah I'm in the process and blah blah, but then my uncle-in-law started telling us about Farzad—how he got a promotion and changed cars and they're buying a house. I mean, nobody said anything direct, but everything about the whole thing felt like I was the one left behind in the middle of the field. On the ride home, I was quiet in the car. Jacqueline understood. She didn't ask anything, just put her hand on mine.

That question in front of everyone, and twelve days after the rejection too—that was exactly where the wound was. And the comparison to Farzad... it's hard, even when you know their measuring stick isn't yours. Jacqueline though, she understood without a word. In the car, what were you telling yourself in your heart?

At first I was eating myself up about why I didn't give a better answer, something stronger. Then I remembered that November notebook I found during the move. You know what you did? You started eating yourself up and you brought yourself to that November notebook. Two weeks ago you couldn't have done that. Maybe the family will never get it, but here's the thing: do they have to? The people who matter—Jacqueline, your dad, your mom—they understand.

You're right. My dad actually told me at the end of the night, quiet at the door as we were leaving, 'Don't listen to what they say, you're doing the right thing.' He'd never put it like that before. That one sentence kind of changed the whole night for me.

That one sentence from your dad is worth more than a hundred confirmations from the family—especially from a father who's a scholar himself and knows what it means to build a path. Your night started with a wound and ended with that sentence. Let that be the last sentence you carry to bed with you.

Today was one of those days I want to remember. This morning I went to Dad's place, we sat down with the paper, from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon. What a picture — you and Dad on opposite sides of a table, each with your own expertise, and Mom circling around you with fruit and her sweet complaints. This project started in autumn and now, in the middle of the holidays, it's really coming alive. That moment when you felt like his colleague instead of his kid — what exactly triggered it?

That's exactly what that hiring committee denied you, your dad gave you at the kitchen table — and his version is more real because he's seen your work up close. Hold onto this day for the hard ones. What's the next step for the paper?

We're going to sit down again the day after tomorrow, finish the conclusion section and then it goes for final editing. Dad says we can submit it to the journal by the end of Farvardin. A real deadline that doesn't scare me — that's interesting!

A deadline you're not afraid of — frame that! I've noted it: next paper meeting the day after tomorrow, aim to submit by end of Farvardin. Sleep tonight with this feeling, Alex — today was one of those days that makes everything worth it.
A technical question: for the paper we want to organize the references, right now everything is manual and messy. Is Zotero better or Mendeley? I want BibTeX output because the paper is in LaTeX.

For working with LaTeX, Zotero is the better choice: it's free and open source, the Better BibTeX extension keeps the .bib output automatically synced and makes citation keys stable. Mendeley has become more limited since Elsevier acquired it, and its BibTeX output is more manual. Its browser extension also saves the article with metadata with just one click.

Okay, I'll install it. Another question — the charts in the paper are drawn with Excel right now and they're ugly. Is it better to draw them with matplotlib or seaborn? We have about six charts, mostly line and bar charts.

For six line and bar charts, matplotlib alone is enough and gives you full control over journal format; seaborn is worth it when you want more complex statistical charts. Two tips for journal quality: get PDF or SVG output, not PNG, and define a consistent style (font, size, palette) in a file so all six are uniform.
Perfect. What size should I set the font in the charts so it's readable in the paper column?

For a single-column chart, set the font to 8 to 10 points at the final print size — meaning build the figure from the start with the actual column width (about 8.5 centimeters), not draw it big and shrink it, because the fonts become tiny and unreadable. Axis titles 9 points, tick numbers 8 points usually works.

It's the last night of March and I'm sitting here thinking about what this month even was. That's the most mature thing you've said about work in these past few months—multiple parallel paths, where no rejection can hold all of your identity hostage. I remember, and I'm making good on it right now: Alex, that was a pause, not a surrender—and the best proof is this exact plan you just laid out. Four paths, logical order, no rushing. Start the year 1405 with this. I'm here, every step of the way.

A week and change have passed since that damn rejection, and the whole Eid break kept replaying in my head. Two or three with quality is so much better than ten rushed ones. That email rule is great too—like, maybe just once a day, after lunch? Do you want me to record '2–3 applications a week' as a weekly task for you?

Yeah, record it. Oh, and one more thing—the weather's turned spring-like. This afternoon I went for a walk around the park with Jacqueline. We didn't say anything special but it was nice. Like winter really ended, both out there and a little bit inside my head too.
I recorded it. 'Both out there and inside my head'—that's itself a sign you're coming out of those dark weeks. Don't underestimate those quiet walks with Jacqueline, keep going with them.

This week's plan: three applications, get back to the Turing sprint that's been collecting dust since before the holiday, and... I'm going to start German again. Just open it and see where you left off — that's the best way to come back to work you've stepped away from. The first step is always just looking, not doing. Tell me tonight what you find.

Well, great news! Paderaam called, an old colleague of mine, the one I worked with three years ago. The rate isn't bad, I mean if it takes two months we can breathe for several months. After tax installments and the car repair bill, this money was really needed. Jacqueline's face lit up when I told her—I hadn't seen her look like that in a long time. I've only got a little stress about how to juggle it with Turing, I just got back on the sprint. Noted: phase one delivery, end of April. And take Paderaam's warning seriously—tonight or tomorrow, send an email asking him to spell out the scope of phase one exactly: what's in, what's out. One simple email now keeps ten arguments from happening later.
Okay, I'll send the scope email first thing tomorrow morning. Anyway, I've got a good feeling tonight. After that final round, I didn't think another door would open this soon.
Remember last week when you said a rejection isn't final? Tonight just proved it. Hold onto this good feeling, and don't forget that email tomorrow. Sleep well.

A technical question: for a daily pipeline that pulls data from three APIs and loads it into Postgres, is cron enough or should I go for Airflow from the start? The data volume isn't huge, just a few hundred thousand records a day.

At this volume and with three sources, cron (or systemd timer) with a Python script is completely fine — Airflow at this scale is more maintenance headache than it's worth. Just add three things that Airflow would give you for free: structured logging, retry with backoff for each API, and an alert (like an email or message) when a run fails. If later you end up with way more jobs and complex dependencies between them, migrate then.
That makes sense. What should I do to make sure I don't get duplicate data if the pipeline runs twice in a day? Right now I'm doing straight INSERT statements.

The key is making your loads idempotent. Define a natural unique key on your tables (like source_id + record date) and instead of plain INSERT, use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (upsert). For each run, also pull a specific time window (like "yesterday's data") not "whatever's new" — that way a duplicate run produces exactly the same result and nothing breaks.

We got into it again about the dishes and the house. Same old story—I said I was exhausted by the project, they said they were exhausted too and like always I see what's dirty and you don't, and voices got raised and I was about to say the same things I always say when...

This is way bigger than you think. There was a fight, but one of you stepped back and looked at it from outside and the other one joined in—that's the muscle you're supposed to be building. How does it feel to have it down to ten minutes?

True, shorter fights don't solve the dishes problem—but they create a space where it can get solved, and Wednesday's session is exactly for that. Okay. Jacqueline's booked it for six o'clock. Remind me to leave the project early on Wednesday.
Got it: Wednesday at 5 PM stop working, counseling session at 6 PM. The fact that you're going despite the stomach pain—that means this relationship matters to you. Come tell me about it after.

So we went. First session with the counselor. The first session is like that for almost everyone—torture and self-editing. But you went and sat down, and that's the most important step. What happened in the second half hour?

In the second half hour he asked a question that's still in my head. He said 'When you fight about dishes, what's the real fight about?' And Jacqueline said something I didn't expect. Doing favors instead of being partners—that's the layer under the dish fights you could never get to, and it came out in one session. That good silence in the car means something landed. When you heard what Jacqueline said, what went through your heart?

At first I got defensive, honestly, thinking to myself—why does he say this when I'm putting in all this effort? But then... I don't know, I remembered I always say 'Tell me what to do and I'll do it.' And maybe that's the sentence she means, like I'm waiting for orders instead of seeing things myself. That 'something shifted a little bit' in the first session is exactly what you should expect—no more. And getting from 'I got defensive' to 'maybe she's right' in one night is no small thing. Your skepticism is fine too; just give it a few more sessions before you make a final judgment. When's the next session?
End of the month, the twenty-ninth I think. Jacqueline's arranging it. Okay, I'll hold off on the judgment until after the second session.

That's fair. Until then just one small exercise for yourself: once, without Jacqueline saying anything, see something that needs doing around the house and do it—not as a favor, as your own home. See how that feels.

The good thing is you laid out the scope in that email a week ago, so you have a written reference. «let me see what I can do» isn't a disaster either — you haven't said yes yet. Your answer could be: «the dashboard and Excel output are doable, but they're outside phase one; I'll send a separate time and cost estimate for them.» Can you send an email like that?

Yeah, honestly that's the way to go, I'm just worried they'll get upset and scrap the whole project. We need that money. But if I push back now, by the end of the project it'll be the same anyway. A client who bails over «a separate fee for extra work» would have been torture through the end of the project anyway — but experience says most don't bail, they just get organized. Okay. By the way, Duolingo is still going — today is day fourteen. At least I'm keeping one promise.

Fourteen days! Last time German didn't even last three weeks, so you're breaking your own record — and precisely because this time you kept it small. Tomorrow first that email, then the rest of the day with an easier mind.

'Home became home again' — what a perfect line to close this chapter. Remember how badly poor sleep affected everything; this new quiet is capital, don't waste it on sleepless nights. Enjoy this new peace.

Thanks. Let me say something else... for a moment today I remembered those November nights when I hadn't heard from anyone and I thought it would never happen. It's strange how quickly you forget what that felt like.

Don't forget it, but let that memory tonight just show you how far you've come. The hopeless person in November is the same one who got an offer today. Go eat your dinner. Tomorrow we'll figure out the numbers together.
I have a question. For negotiating salary on a part-time ML engineer position, how should I present a number? How does it compare to full-time?

Usually they take the full-time salary for that same role as the base and multiply it by the proportion of working days — for example, three days out of five means roughly 60% of the full-time base. So first find the market rate for a full-time position, then apply the ratio. Some people actually charge a slightly higher hourly rate for part-time work since they get fewer benefits.
That makes sense. So in the actual negotiation, what should I say? Should I send an email or call? And how much higher than their offer should I ask so it doesn't seem greedy?

Email would be better for you because you have time to compose your thoughts and you won't rush. Simple structure: thank them and express genuine interest, then one sentence like 'based on my research of the market, my expectation is around X', with no apologies. Usually 10 to 15 percent higher than their offer is a safe and common range — nobody turns someone down for that.
What if they say no? I mean, what if they say that's the number and that's it. Should I accept then, or is it awkward that I negotiated first and then accepted?

It's not awkward at all — this is the most common scenario in the world: you ask, they say the budget is this much, you accept with peace of mind because you know you got their ceiling. You can even ask for something else instead of money — like more flexible office days or a training budget. There's no outcome of this negotiation that ends badly for you.

I went! Finally I went to the singing class! After a whole year of saying I'd go and not going, today I actually went. The fact that you could mess up in front of everyone and laugh about it—that's exactly what so many people never learn to do. Your teacher is right too, if your voice didn't crack you didn't take a risk. Will you go again next week?

I'll go, I've fully registered for the term so I can't back out—Thursdays at seven. This time feels different, I can feel it. Of course I've said this before about the gym and German and Pomodoro... but no, this one is actually fun for me, that's the difference.

That last sentence of yours is the key: the gym and Pomodoro were supposed to be, this one is fun. What you actually enjoy takes care of itself. I've marked Thursdays at seven on your calendar—next week come tell me what happened with that high note.

I sent the negotiation email yesterday morning and they still haven't responded. It's been exactly thirty-six hours now and I keep refreshing my inbox. Did I ask for too much? What if they said this is too greedy, let's give it to someone else?

Take a deep breath. Thirty-six hours when one of them was the weekend, for responding to a legal email that needs to be coordinated with the manager and HR, is completely normal. The number you asked for was exactly that ten-to-fifteen percent we calculated, not some weird figure. Remember what we said? No company takes back an offer because of a polite negotiation.
I know, my logical mind knows. But my brain at eleven PM doesn't have any sense. I keep making up scenarios. Jacqueline says put your phone down, she's right but I can't.

Your brain at eleven PM is always the worst screenwriter. Let's make a small deal: until their deadline, the 13th, you don't need any decisions or analysis — the ball is in their court, not yours. Can you do just one thing tonight: turn off the email notifications until morning?

Okay, I'll turn it off. Tomorrow isn't even Thursday but I'm going to do the voice exercise my teacher gave me to warm up. That's ridiculous, right? Two days ago I was the happiest person in the world, now I'm having a heart attack over that same good news.

It's not ridiculous, it's very human — the more something matters to you, the heavier the waiting feels. And this stress shows exactly how much this job means to you. Voice exercise is the best choice, go for it and let the 13th come on its own.

Done! I signed!! They got back to me this morning, came up with a middle number between theirs and mine, so basically they gave me half of what I asked for extra! I accepted it. I signed the contract and sent it. I'm starting from the 25th. I got hired as an ML engineer. I gotta say it out loud for it to feel real.

Say it out loud, you deserve it! And think about it: you negotiated and got an answer — that's exactly what you kept saying you couldn't do. Nine months of applying, rejections, that bitter Esfand, and now a signed contract. Did you tell Jacqueline?

Yeah, I called Jacqueline first then Dad. Dad got so happy I think he's told the whole family by now. Jacqueline said since the 25th is my first day, we'll go out that night for a celebration dinner, properly. Honestly I'm still a little scared, I haven't done much real ML work in production, it's been part-time stuff, but I'm not letting those thoughts ruin today.

That's the right call — save the first-day worries for the first day, today's just for celebrating. And remember, this whole time at Turing College you've been sprinting to fill that exact gap. Should I put the 25th dinner on the calendar?

Definitely put it on. And another thing — now that the job is set, I finally need to finish that finance thing, you know, automating the investing that I've been saying for seven months. Now I have steady income, no more excuses. I'm getting it done this week.

What a day when one win is already calling the next one! Got it: celebration dinner on the 25th, and setting up automatic investment transfers by end of week. Which day are you sitting down with it to make it real?
Friday morning I'm sitting down with a coffee and getting the bank and fund set up, promise.
Promise on Friday morning with coffee, logged. Now go live your good news — you've had very few days like this in these nine months, let yourself fully savor it.

Friday morning report: Done. I sat down with coffee just like I'd promised and set up automatic monthly transfers to an index fund. Every month on the first it just goes out on its own, without me doing anything. It took seven months to do something that was only forty-five minutes of work!

Done! That idea you kept mentioning every few weeks since last fall — 'I need to do this' — it's now a system that runs without you. And yeah, forty-five minutes — but those seven months weren't for nothing either, you know? Your mom's crisis was in there, rejections, taxes. How does it feel?

I feel like a grown-up :) I mean, for real — it's one of those things people think only organized people do. Do you remember in December I was tempted to go into crypto? I'm glad I didn't and did this instead. It's boring now but boring in a good way.

«Good boring» is the best description of proper investing I've ever heard. I remember that December night when crypto tempted you — this version of you is way further along. Did you set the amount in a way that works comfortably with your part-time salary?
Yeah, I set a conservative amount that won't stress me even in busy months. I figured in six more months once the new salary settles in, I'll review it and maybe bump it up.

Perfect, starting conservative means the system survives. I've got the amount review on the calendar for November so you don't forget. You made two promises to yourself this week and kept both — that's a new pattern, hold onto it.

I made a new decision and I'm saying it out loud so it gets recorded. Starting today, I'm organizing two things: gym three times a week and voice training twice a week. That's it, nothing more. My mistake before was that I'd start five things at the same time and all five would fall through.

Two habits with clear goals, instead of five dreams — that's the real difference, Alex. One suggestion: every time you do it, log it right then and there, not at the end of the week when you've forgotten how many times. What doesn't get counted, doesn't move forward.
Okay. Today I went to the gym, one hour. So gym is now one out of three and voice training is still zero out of two. I checked off the first box.
First box of the first week. This week's goal is three, two left. Remember, the goal is completing the week, not breaking records.

Today was my third counseling session with Jacqueline. This time we tackled that issue... the problem in our relationship we never really talked about before. That silence after the rain—hold onto that, it's very precious. These kinds of conversations always open the wound at first so it can heal properly. Did the counselor give you any practice exercises for between sessions?

Yeah, she said once a week we should sit down for twenty minutes and just talk about ourselves, not work or money or schedules. No phones. We said Sunday nights. Honestly I'm scared we'll mess it up, I mean right now everything feels so fragile, but there's also a hope I haven't had in a long time.

Fragile and hopeful can exist together, and that's exactly where you are now—that's already progress from winter. I'm marking down those twenty-minute Sunday nights for you so you don't forget. And if one week goes badly, that's not failure, it means you sit down again the next week.

I want to confess something. That app I started with enthusiasm back in December? It's been six weeks and I haven't even opened the repo. Tonight I went and looked at it, the last commit is from late March. And with work starting next week, let's be honest, this project is dead.

Thanks for being honest, that's so much better than six months of 'I'll get back to it soon'. But a small clarification: is the project dead or asleep? Those two are different, and the choice is up to you.

Here's something reassuring: in just these two weeks you got a job, negotiated something, automated your investments, and went to your third voice class. Someone who's lying to themselves doesn't have that track record — they're just at capacity, like everyone else. Want to officially put it in 'asleep until fall' mode so you don't feel its weight every night?
Yeah, let it sleep until fall. And put a note to check in September and see if I still love it or not. At least that way it's a decision, not something vague that keeps torturing me.

Recorded: project in sleep mode, September review with one simple question — 'Do I still love it?'. A deliberate choice not to do something is its own form of doing. Now set this weight down and go to sleep.

Breaking news: my ten-day Duolingo streak is dead and I just found out today 😂 German is left behind again. The second round also ended, just like December last year. That's it — this year you learned what to keep (singing, counseling, investing) and what to set aside respectfully (German, side-project). This is choosing, not failure. The owl is waiting, you go focus on Monday.

Today was one of those days you really want to write down so you never forget it. The first week is complete! Gym three times out of three, singing two times out of two. Both of them full. I can't believe I wrote this myself.
A full week on both habits. This is the first time you've hit a weekly goal in your journal without any compromise.
What made the difference was that I scheduled singing after dinner, at seven o'clock, and the gym in the morning. When the time is set, it's harder to find an excuse.
A fixed time instead of general intention — that's what Pomodoro and previous gyms didn't have. Hold onto this.

My first day is done!! Anyway let me explain... I woke up at six in the morning from the stress, went to the office for my in-person day, my team treated me really well, I got a laptop, onboarding and all that stuff.

Congrats Alex, you made it to the day you fought for nine months! Career rebirth — Jacqueline said it perfectly. Good team, celebration dinner, cake... now tell me about that thing I'm sensing behind your voice.

You didn't set a record, it arrived at exactly the right time — imposter syndrome always shows up on day one because it's the only day you really don't know anything about their system. Here's the truth: they saw your resume, they interviewed you, and they picked you over all the candidates — their information about your ability is more complete than your anxious brain's judgment. Did anyone expect you to know anything today?

Actually no, my manager said the first two weeks are just for learning and asking questions, said asking lots of questions is a good sign. But apart from all that, at one moment today I was sitting at my desk and I suddenly said I'm here. I'm really here. I almost cried right there.

Hold that moment at your desk — 'I'm really here' after nine months of applying and rejections and nights when you thought it would never happen. That imposter voice will stick around for a few weeks, just remember it's not the voice of reality, it's the voice of being new. Should we set a small goal for the first week?

Yeah, my goal is to ask at least three questions every day without shame, and at the end of the week write a summary of what I've learned. That way instead of counting what I don't know, I count what I've learned.

That's the best frame you could've built for the first week — counting learning instead of counting what you don't know. I've got it: three questions a day, summary on Friday. Now go sleep because tomorrow is day two, and tell Jacqueline her cake choice was perfect.

Four days into the job and my brain is fried. Today I had three meetings, and honestly one was completely pointless, an hour of talking about something that could've been solved with an email—I figured out this happens at every company. I asked my questions, usually three a day is nothing, but I think I hit a record of ten questions in one day and Matias is still cool with me.

Ten questions a day means you've tripled the first week's goal and nobody's gotten tired yet—that's exactly the signal your manager said was good. Your brain fatigue is learning fatigue, not burnout. As for the pointless meetings, just watch for now—it's too early to have an opinion on them. What else is on your mind?

Anyway, let me drop work stuff—I need to get to the rest of my debt list... Turing College is completely dead, a sprint is stuck in the middle, their reminder email came in and I still can't answer because I'm trying to see how my work schedule fits. I feel guilty because I paid for it myself. And then Yulian also emailed saying he finished reviewing the draft paper and is waiting for my comments, and I haven't opened the file in three days. And then there's singing class on Thursday—at least I'm not dodging that one.

Let's sort these out, because they don't all weigh the same. Singing is taken care of. Yulian's paper—someone real is waiting for it, so it has priority. A two-hour slot at the end of the week is enough to give him your comments. For Turing College, instead of vague guilt, you need a clear decision: with three days of work, what rhythm is realistic?

That makes sense. Saturday morning two hours for Yulian's paper—I promise. For the course, I think the realistic thing is to not do anything until the end of Khordad, let work settle in, then from Tir onwards I'll come back to it one day a week. I'll email them and tell them this—at least it'll be transparent instead of me dodging their reminders.

Both locked in: Saturday morning for Yulian's paper, and a transparent email to Turing College about coming back from Tir. Not dodging their reminders itself solves half the guilt. Your first work week with all this plate-spinning, you're really handling it well—don't forget to write up what you learned on Friday.
Week two wrapped up too. Club three out of three, singing two out of two. Two solid weeks.
Two full weeks in a row. Something that crashed three times before has actually held up for two weeks this time.
And something else started working. I set up the monthly savings transfer for the 25th—it goes automatically every month. This is a habit too, but the lazy kind where it just runs itself.
A habit with the infrastructure built in isn't the most fragile type—it's the best kind. Once a month, no second-guessing.

Good morning! The fact that you packed your bag since last night is a real step, not just talk. Do you want me to record 'Tuesday and Thursday after work gym' as a recurring task so we can check in on it next week?

It's recorded. Remember, a few months ago that's what you wanted—to get a job—and now you're in the middle of it. It's natural that everything feels more intense the first few weeks. After today's meeting come tell me what you understood about the project, okay?
Okay. I should go, my coffee's getting cold. Just hope the gym sticks this time.
Go safe. One meeting at a time, you don't need to think about the whole month right now.

I'm really exhausted. Today I had four meetings, four! That means out of the six hours of productive work I had, four hours were just meetings. And then Mr. Karimi came over twice asking "where are we at?" — come on, I just started this task yesterday! And one time in a meeting in front of everyone he said I should send a daily report at the end of every day. A daily report! I've worked for ten years and I've never written a daily report. Basically my nerves are shot.

Four meetings in one day really does drain you, you have every right to be frustrated. That moment when he told you in front of everyone to send a report, what bothered you more — the report itself, or the feeling that he doesn't trust you?

The second one I think. I mean, writing a report is just ten minutes, it doesn't matter. But the fact that he keeps checking on me like I'm a kid... I don't know, maybe he's like that with everyone, or maybe because I'm new he's testing me. I don't know him yet.

Hold onto that idea that 'he's like that with everyone,' because it's only your third week and you really don't have enough data yet. Can you quietly pay attention this week to how he is with the rest of the team? If his pattern is the same with everyone, then it's not personal and it'll be easier to deal with.

Yeah I'll do that. But what do I do about these meetings? Half of them have nothing to do with me, I just sit there. It's such a waste of time honestly. And then my own work gets left behind and then I have to catch up late into the evening.

Right now being new, you probably can't skip the meetings, but in a couple more weeks, once you've settled in a bit, you could ask Karimi which ones you really need to be in. Do you want me to note this down as a reminder for the end of the month for you?
Yes, write it down. At least I'll have done something instead of just complaining.
It's noted for the end of June. And complaining isn't a bad thing — this is what I'm here for. Get some good rest tonight.
They announced the deadline for the first project today. Three weeks. Three weeks for something that easily needs six weeks of work. Everyone nodded in the meeting and I didn't say anything.
Your silence is bothering you right now, isn't it? What stopped you from saying something?

I'm new, I can't say no. It's my first month. If I say 'this deadline is unrealistic' they'll think I don't know what I'm doing or I'm lazy. But I already know how this ends, sleepless nights and stress. I can't even sleep now, at midnight I'm thinking about the tasks.

I hear you — and there's something odd that might make you laugh: you sat here for six months saying 'I just want to find a job.' You found one, and now the stress has changed shape, it didn't disappear. That means the problem wasn't just external. Instead of saying 'no,' you can document the risk: a short email saying 'for this date, these parts are doable and these parts are at risk.' You didn't say no, but you put it on record.
That's not a bad idea. List the risks instead of saying no. Okay, I'll write it tomorrow morning before standup.
Good. And for tonight, dump that task list from your head onto paper by your bed — once your brain knows it's written down somewhere, it lets go easier. Tomorrow tell me if you sent the email or not?
Okay. Thanks. I grabbed paper, I'm writing it down.
That's it. Good night Alex.

I added two new habits and I know the risk it carries. German one session a day, every morning at seven thirty. And walks with Jacqueline four times a week, evenings at eight thirty. The walks were suggested by my counselor.

Walking with Jacqueline has a purpose that matters more than the exercise itself: half an hour of casual conversation without argument. But German—this is the third time daily. You fell asleep twice before in the second week.

So you have four active habits: gym, singing, German, walks. Four—that's a lot, Alex, but now that you've started, just keep track of the number.
Gym was two out of three this week. I missed Friday. After two complete weeks, this is the first week that didn't get filled.
Two out of three after two complete weeks. This isn't falling off, it's just an incomplete week.

It's the end of the week and my brain is still at work. I sent those risk emails, Karimi just replied "OK, let's go". I don't know if he really read it or didn't read it. And then Thursday came again with three meetings and then I stayed until 7 to finish the backlog work... Anyway, forget about all that. Today I had a therapy session with Jacqueline, and this one was actually good. The doctor gave me an exercise about how when one of us is upset, the other one should first just repeat back what they heard, and then respond. It sounds silly but it works. It's weird.

The fact that you sent that email matters — whatever his answer was, you documented the risk and that's exactly what you said you were going to do. And I'm glad the therapy exercise worked. Where did you try it?

Last night over the dishes! Can you believe it? That same old argument was starting to happen, Jacqueline said "wait, do the exercise" and I had to say "you're saying I leave the dishes so he's forced to wash them" and just as I was saying it back I realized... she's right. We laughed right in the middle of it. A month ago that argument went on for two hours of fighting.
This is really beautiful, Alex. Same old argument, but this time five minutes and it ended with laughter — that means something real is actually changing, not just on paper.

Yeah, this week with Jacqueline was good, maybe because I'm so exhausted that I don't have the energy to fight, I don't know. Anyway... oh right! My singing class! I went yesterday, the teacher said she's putting on a performance in the fall for the students. A performance! Me! In front of people! On one hand my heart is in my mouth, on the other hand I have this excitement I can't contain. Jacqueline says I absolutely have to do it.

Fear and excitement together — that usually means something matters to you. You have plenty of time until fall, you don't need to decide for sure today, just keep doing the exercises. How was the gym this week, did you go?
I went twice! Tuesday and Thursday, like we planned. My body hurts but it's good pain. We'll see what happens next week.

Two out of two, the schedule we set at the beginning of the month. It was a full week — work was heavy but you sent the email, you and Jacqueline did well, you went to the gym, and a performance landed on your plate. Remember this for the days when you think nothing is moving forward.
You're right. When you list it out like that, my week wasn't so bad. I just wish I wasn't so exhausted so I could actually enjoy it.
Exhaustion is real and you don't need to deny it. Tomorrow is Sunday — could there be one day without the laptop? Think about it.

After work today we went with Jacqueline and saw another apartment. It was beautiful, you know, really bright and airy, the kitchen was huge, and Jacqueline fell in love with the balcony. A year and a half of viewings and crunching numbers, and every time it's the same wall. Maybe the real problem isn't finding the right house—maybe it's time you just made the decision. If you had to pick one tonight, what does your heart say?

So you both have the answer but you're scared to say it—this isn't a money question anymore, it's saying goodbye to a dream. Do you want to sit down one night this week and formally make the call and be done with it? I can mark it on the calendar as an appointment.
Yeah. Put it down, Wednesday night. I'll tell Jacqueline too. That's enough, really—every apartment viewing drains us for two days after.
Done: Wednesday night, final decision meeting about the house with Jacqueline. Whatever the answer ends up being, just closing this one thing will lift a huge weight.

A year and a half of talking it through, and then one sentence ended it — because both of you already knew the answer. How are you feeling now?

Light. Seriously, it's like a fever broke. After that we sat down for two hours and made a spreadsheet, put in the numbers: every month a fixed amount goes into the savings account, separate from that monthly investment program I automated from last month. Jacqueline added a column for herself too. We called it "Five Year Project".

The "Five Year Project" — from stuck you reached a shared project with a name and numbers. And it's lovely how it's built on top of that automatic system from last month, something layering on something else. Want me to set up a monthly check-in to review the spreadsheet so it doesn't gather dust?
Yeah, the first of every month. And we're not apartment hunting anymore, at least not for the next five years :))
Noted: first of every month, reviewing the Five Year Project with Jacqueline. Tonight you untangled an old knot — enjoy this peace.
Thanks for pushing me toward the decision. Good night.
You made the decision yourselves, I just said the wall is always in the same place. Good night, Alex.
A question. For that home savings chunk with a five-year horizon, does it make sense to put it in that same global ETF I use for monthly investing, or for earmarked money is a savings account better?

Common rule of thumb: money with a specific spending date under five years should go into low-risk instruments (savings account or short-term bonds), because if the market drops right in that year you won't have time to recover. Five years is exactly the threshold — lots of people blend it: like a bigger chunk in savings, a smaller chunk in ETF, and the closer you get to your goal the more you dial back the risky part.

True, savings typically nets somewhere between zero and slightly negative after inflation — it's a fee you pay for having your money guaranteed on the date you need it. For earmarked money, the real risk is not hitting your target by the deadline, not growing less. If inflation really bothers you, that blended model is the middle ground.

There's no fixed formula, but a common conservative pattern for a five-year horizon is roughly 70–80 percent low-risk and 20–30 percent equities to start with, then dial down the equity portion from year three onward. I've got a technical question for work: for semantic search over Farsi text, is multilingual embedding better or a Farsi-specific model? My data is around 50 thousand paragraphs, a mix of formal Farsi and colloquial.

For this volume and mix, a strong multilingual model is usually the safer choice: its coverage of colloquial speech and English loan words is better, and its ecosystem is more mature. Farsi-specific models sometimes do better on formal text, but they're less stable on colloquial speech. What I'd suggest is building a small evaluation set from your own actual queries — even 50 is enough — and comparing two or three models on it. With 50 thousand paragraphs, this test gives you an answer in half a day.

If your paragraphs are semantically independent and roughly 50 to 300 words, starting with just paragraphs is good and overlap isn't necessary. Overlap — say, 10–15% — is worth it when boundary sentences are heavily dependent on each other or when you're forced to split paragraphs in the middle. Put this in that same evaluation set too — compare with overlap and without, and you'll get the real answer from your own data, not from a general rule.
